item.title: The miracle cure in your Facebook feed is killing Bangladeshis. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Every Bangladeshi family knows the scene. My father is newly diagnosed with diabetes. The doctor's advice is the same as always: Medication, diet, regular monitoring, lifelong discipline. It is sound advice, and it is exhausting to follow.
Then his morning walk friend forwards a video to him. A man in a white coat promises a cure in seven days, with no injections and no side effects, for only Tk3,500 and cash on delivery.
This is not harmless chatter. It is a business, and its customers are dying.
Diabetes is a lifelong condition for which no cure currently exists. That inconvenient truth is the foundation of a thriving commercial ecosystem on Facebook and TikTok: Fake doctors, unregistered supplements, and "miracle" pills sold to people who are frightened, tired, or simply priced out of regular care.
Social media is filled with products claiming to replace insulin or conventional medication with herbal alternatives, despite no credible scientific evidence supporting those claims. Patients each month require hospitalization after following unqualified health advice found on social media and resulting in liver, kidney, or cardiovascular complications.
Think about what that number means. Families continue to pay for someone else's marketing copy with their organs. Now think about the patients who never made it to a hospital.
The word "herbal" does a great deal of the sellers' work. In a country with a long and respected tradition of traditional remedies, "natural" feels "safe." It is not.
A product with no declared dose, no tested purity, and no registration is simply an unknown substance. The danger is greatest when a patient stops a prescribed drug because a post told them they no longer need it.
What makes this scam distinctly Bangladeshi is how skilfully it borrows trust. Fraudsters know we respect the doctor, the professor, and the familiar newspaper masthead, so they counterfeit all three.
Dr Jahangir Kabir, a prominent health advocate who promotes lifestyle-based approaches to diabetes, has said dishonest groups are misusing his name to sell unregulated medicines.
He reports that hundreds of fake Facebook pages were created in his name, some even mimicking his verified profile's blue-badge image. A man who tells people to change how they eat and live found his face on the label of a bottle.
He is not alone. Microbiologist Dr Senjuti Saha discovered that her name and image were being used in a fraudulent campaign and filed a general diary at the police station.
Dismislab traced the "Optimax" diabetes product to counterfeit pages mimicking Prothom Alo, featuring fake interviews with "prominent" Bangladeshi professionals.
Even the health minister's identity has been hijacked: iIn 2024 the ministry had to warn that fake Facebook accounts were being opened in his name, with advertisements that could cheat the public.
When the scammer can wear the face of a trusted doctor and the logo of a trusted newspaper, "just don't believe everything online" is not advice. It is an abdication.
We have long assumed that more smartphones meant more awareness. The evidence is more troubling. Studies suggest that mobile phone ownership is associated with greater exposure to misinformation, not just greater access to information.
In a country where phones have reached the village before the specialist has, the same device that delivers a telemedicine consultation also delivers a "cure" for diabetes. In many cases, it is the second that arrives first.
Self-medication was already common long before Facebook. We buy tablets over the counter, trust a neighbour's prescription, and stretch a doctor's visit as far as it will go. Influencers did not create this habit. They have simply learned to monetize it.
Media professionals are not blameless. For years our response to health misinformation has been the occasional "myth-buster" column, published once, read by few, and forgotten by the next news cycle. The scammers publish daily. We cannot answer a daily campaign with an annual correction.
Newspapers need standing health fact-check desks, with trained reporters, a medical advisory panel, and the same institutional seriousness we give to political fact-checking. A fake diabetes ad should be treated with the same urgency as a fake political quote.
Television channels and online portals should produce short, shareable "spot the scam" segments in Bangla. Sixty seconds are enough to show a viewer how to check whether a doctor is registered with the Bangladesh Medical and Dental Council, why "cure in seven days" is a warning rather than a promise, and why no pill replaces insulin. Content that is easy to forward to the family WhatsApp group is how we compete on the scammers' own ground.
We should use AI sensibly. Newsrooms can deploy language tools, including Bangla-capable ones, to flag viral health claims, repeated ad creatives, and suspicious pages at a scale no human desk can match.
But AI should only flag. Verification, context, and the final call must remain with trained editors and doctors. A machine can tell us where the fire is. It cannot tell us whether the person in the video is really a physician.
Finally, the media must stop accepting the framing that this is merely a "content moderation" problem. Content moderation means a platform deciding whether a post stays up.
What we are describing is the sale of unregistered medicinal products, under false identities, to sick people, for profit. That is consumer fraud and a public health offense.
The Directorate General of Drug Administration, the Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulatory Commission, the consumer rights authorities and law enforcement all have a role.
So do Meta and TikTok, which earn revenue from the very advertisements that deceive our citizens.
The press should keep asking the uncomfortable questions: Who approved this ad, who was paid, who was prosecuted, and how many times was it reported before it came down?
The next time a "miracle cure" appears in your feed, remember what it is: Someone's sales pitch, aimed at your parent's fear.
Insulin is not a conspiracy, and diabetes does not end in seven days. The sooner we say so, loudly, every single day, the fewer families will learn it in a hospital corridor.
Dewan Shahnoor Alam Sourav is a lecturer in the Department of Media Studies and Journalism at the University of Liberal Arts Bangladesh (ULAB). Can be reached at ds.alam.sourav@gmail.com .

item.title: How do I grieve someone I have not met yet?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
This is what I kept asking myself as I waited in the hospital, knowing that my 4.5-month pregnancy was coming to an end. Perhaps it is simply human nature to grow attached to the life growing inside you.
My entire life, I have catastrophized everything. The same happened when I found out I was pregnant. But I quickly tried to quiet that part of me and focus on doing my best.
Everything was going perfectly. I had no known risk factors, my scans had gone well, and my doctor had told me to schedule an appointment for the following month.
No one had warned me that even when everything seemed to be going well, it could all turn upside down in the blink of an eye.
I had gone to sleep when my amniotic fluid ruptured. Even half asleep, I knew what that meant. My pregnancy had ended. I was rushed to the hospital, and the duty doctor tried to console me: “We do not know yet.”
But I knew that the future I had already started imagining would no longer come to be.
I had to wait an excruciating 12 hours for my gynaecologist to examine me. She finally explained what would happen next. I would be given one dose of medication that day and more the following day to induce labour.
Miscarriage . Just one word, carrying a weight that is almost impossible to put into words. A grief so profound, yet one no one warns you about.
While I waited in the hospital for the procedures to be completed, my aunts, uncles, grandmothers, cousins, everyone, rallied around me. I was going through one of the most difficult periods of my life, but I was wrapped in a blanket of love.
The women around me told me their own stories of loss, their struggles, and how they had found a way through. Even though my own pain felt insurmountable, it was the strength I found in their stories that helped me through.
Despite medical science coming such a long way, no reason could be identified for why this was happening to me. The pregnancy was not advanced enough for there to be any hope of saving it, but it was also not early enough for my miscarriage to go unnoticed.
The medication I was given sent my body into what felt like a state of shock. I was shivering uncontrollably, and when the shivering stopped, my body would have to endure contractions. I had to feel the pain of labour, but there was no baby to hold at the end of it.
Nothing could be done to ease my pain, knowing that there was no possibility of a different ending. I was handed a death certificate for someone who never even had a birth certificate.
It is estimated that one in four to six pregnancies ends in miscarriage. But the statistics are complex. There are a multitude of factors that can play a role.
Most of the websites I have visited state that miscarriages are common. And this makes me question: Why is there so little conversation about something that affects women so deeply?
A pregnancy loss is deeply personal, and it should always be a woman’s prerogative to decide whether she wants to talk about it. But for those who do want to talk about it, do we have enough safe spaces?
There is so little mental health support for women going through a loss like this. I was genuinely grateful for the hospital staff who consoled me, who held my hand when my body was going through unbearable pain, and for the doctors who treated me with respect and dignity. But is that guaranteed for every woman who experiences a loss like this?
Too often, these losses are minimised with statements such as, “It was not meant to be.” As though a few words can make the grief disappear. We should hold space for women who are going through these losses and create more meaningful systems of support.
When even “rich” countries struggle to fund research into miscarriage and pregnancy loss, there is little hope for a country like Bangladesh.
The world can be an extremely cruel place for women. But I refuse to be anything but kind to myself.
There was a version of me that existed before the miscarriage, and there is a version of me that exists now. I do not think they are the same person.
The trivial things in life that used to bother me no longer seem to matter. Things I once thought were important have suddenly lost weight. There is something about losing something so deeply wanted that changes your understanding of what truly matters.
While I do not want my pregnancy loss to define me, I also cannot pretend that it is not a part of who I am now. I will carry this loss with me, and I will not allow it to be swept under the carpet or reduced to something that simply happened and should be forgotten.
I am still grieving the future I do not get to have. There is no linear path through a loss this profound. I was applauded for being brave, but the truth is, I was forced to be brave.
I no longer want to be courageous. I want to mourn. I want to grieve the life I never got to meet, on my own terms.
It is the strength of my parents, partner, and siblings that has kept me going. Life keeps moving forward, even though it felt like mine had stopped for a while.
The only lesson I carry forward is that I will show up with love, strength, and support for any woman who has gone through something similar. There should be more conversations about this reality, about a kind of loss that can be so profound and yet have no logical answers. Women should be allowed to grieve without being told how they should grieve.
Ahona Hassan is a human rights activist passionate about speaking on issues often left unspoken.

item.title: A collective failure. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The tragic loss of at least 20 young lives to suicide following the publication of this year’s SSC and HSC examination results -- including nine deaths within just ten days of the recent HSC announcement -- is a devastating indictment of our society.
Worse still, given the pervasive stigma surrounding mental health and self-harm across the country, these reported figures likely represent only a fraction of the true toll.
When teenagers choose to end their lives over academic scores, it exposes a profound moral and institutional collapse. That we live in a society where exam grades are treated as the sole determinant of human worth is a horrifying reality.
For decades, parents, educators, and communities have conditioned students to believe that falling short of a coveted GPA-5 or failing a board examination equates to absolute ruin. The relentless cycle of parental comparisons, social humiliation, and rigid academic expectations leaves vulnerable young minds isolated and terrified of disappointing their families.
When an examination hall becomes a matter of life and death, the entire pedagogical and social framework has fundamentally broken down. No board certificate is worth a single child's life, yet our culture continues to weaponize academic performance against the emotional well-being of our children.
This crisis demands immediate, structural intervention from both the state and society. We need accessible, confidential psychological counseling services in our educational institutions -- not as a formality, but as an active support network operating before and after exam seasons. Simultaneously, we must also expand emergency crisis helplines and train teachers to recognize early signs of acute distress and isolation.
Beyond policy, families must replace interrogation and shame with empathy and understanding, reassuring their children that academic setbacks are temporary obstacles, not life sentences.
If we continue to prioritize grades over emotional survival, these preventable tragedies will remain an annual stain on our national conscience. We must act now to protect our youth before another promising life is lost to despair.

Time to deliver to climate promises. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and UN General Assembly President Dr Khalilur Rahman both delivered what is an overdue message to the global community: The era of empty climate promises must end.
The prime minister rightly pointed out that climate-vulnerable nations require grants, not debt-inducing loans, all the while outlining five concrete actions to overhaul what must be called a broken international finance architecture.
Simultaneously, Dr Khalilur Rahman warned that the widening disparity between political pledges and real-world implementation has become an existential chasm, urging world leaders to make Antalya the "COP of implementation."
Nowhere is the hypocrisy displayed by the developed world more damaging than across developing countries of the Global South, and on the frontlines of our own country.
While global carbon emissions surged to a record 42 billion tons last year and warming trajectories hurtle toward 2.8 degrees Celsius for this century, developing economies continue bearing the catastrophic brunt of a crisis they did not create.
Bangladesh itself contributes less than 0.5% of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet our coastal communities, river systems, and agricultural yields are being systematically dismantled by rising seas, salinity intrusion, and relentless cyclones.
The financial arithmetic outlined in Antalya lays bare the moral failure of major industrial polluters. Developing countries require up to $305 billion annually merely to adapt to climate fallout, yet international adaptation funding languishes at a paltry $26bn. As the UNGA president aptly noted, that shortfall is not a rounding error but a verdict on global solidarity.
If COP31 is to mean anything, wealthy nations must immediately honour their historical obligations. More international climate finance must be dedicated directly to adaptation, distributed as predictable grants based on vulnerability rather than arbitrary income classifications.
Antalya must not become another venue for hollow declarations. Major carbon-emitting powers must abandon stalling tactics and deliver the finance and action required to safeguard nations such as Bangladesh in the developing world.

item.title: Is our healthcare system built for a climate crisis?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Every monsoon, Dhaka’s hospitals follow a mundane, predictable routine. The corridors at Mugda Medical College Hospital and Dhaka Medical College Hospital overflow with patients burning with high fevers, platelets dropping, and families frantically searching for intravenous fluids and blood donors.
Months later, when floodwaters recede from low-lying districts or a blistering April heatwave descends on the capital, the wards yet again get overcrowded, this time with patients suffering from waterborne illnesses, heatstroke, and acute kidney issues.
We treat each surge as an isolated seasonal emergency, still the common thread tying these crises together is no longer just a pathogen or a sluggish city corporation cleanup drive. It is a rapidly warming and increasingly volatile climate.
And right now, Bangladesh’s healthcare system is fighting a 21st-century climate war with 20th-century, reactive armor.
In real time, climate change is redrawing Bangladesh’s epidemiological map, and the data from our own health system leaves no room for denial.
According to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), dengue has shattered every historical boundary. After the catastrophic 2023 outbreak that saw 321,179 hospitalizations and 1,705 deaths, the crisis has refused to recede into a mere seasonal nuisance.
In 2025, DGHS recorded over 102,800 cases and 413 fatalities and by November 2026, nationwide hospitalizations have already surpassed 155,000, claiming 479 lives, with significant surges extending into post-monsoon autumn and spreading across all 64 districts.
The Aedes mosquito’s breeding cycle gets accelerated with warmer microclimates and erratic rainfall, turning a once-localized monsoon infection into a year-round national emergency.
Meanwhile, the crisis influences far beyond mosquitoes. Along our low-lying coastline in Khulna, Satkhira, and Bagerhat, rising sea levels and intensifying cyclones are driving severe salinity intrusion into freshwater aquifers.
Public health studies in coastal Bangladesh show that residents consuming moderately saline drinking water (above 2,000 mg/L) face a 42% higher risk of developing hypertension compared to those drinking fresh water.
In coastal subdistricts like Dacope, tubewell sodium levels routinely exceed the World Health Organization’s 200 mg/L threshold. It pushes the daily sodium intake from drinking water alone near the WHO’s entire daily limit of 2 grams and driving alarming spikes in gestational hypertension and pre-eclampsia among pregnant women.
Inland, extreme urban heatwaves are turning concrete-heavy cities into thermal traps, pushing emergency rooms past their limits with heat exhaustion and cardiovascular strain.
Our public health apparatus remains trapped in a cycle of crisis management, despite these unmistakable numbers. We wait till the hospital beds overflow, forcing facilities like Mugda Medical College Hospital to scramble to triple their dengue ward capacity mid-outbreak, before declaring an emergency.
Municipalities launch reactive mosquito-fogging campaigns only after community transmission has peaked. Relief teams distribute oral rehydration salts and water-purification tablets after floodwaters have already submerged community clinics and Upazila health complexes.
A reactive system is inherently expensive, tiring, and deadly. By the time an outbreak registers in traditional hospital admissions data, transmission is already out of control. Worse, extreme weather events frequently cripple the very facilities meant to save lives, flooding ground-floor pharmacies, knocking out power grids during severe heatwaves, and severing supply chains for essential medicines.
Building a climate-resilient health system
Transitioning from firefighting to foresight requires two structural shifts in how Bangladesh plans and finances public health:
This means elevating critical infrastructure such as generators, oxygen plants, and medical storage above projected flood levels, integrating solar microgrids to keep cooling systems and life-support running during grid failures, and installing dedicated rainwater harvesting and desalination units in salinity-affected zones, where rainwater has been shown to cut drinking-water sodium exposure by over 95% compared to tubewells.
If meteorological models forecast an unseasonably warm, wet spell, municipalities and hospitals can pre-position IV fluids and NS1 rapid diagnostic kits, deploy targeted larviciding, and alert communities weeks before the first wave of fever patients arrives at the emergency.
Climate change is not a distant environmental abstraction for Bangladesh, it is sitting in our hospital waiting rooms today. Treating every dengue surge, cholera outbreak, and salinity-linked stroke as an unexpected shock guarantees that our doctors will remain overwhelmed and our most vulnerable citizens will pay the price.
If we want a healthcare system capable of surviving the decades ahead, we must stop measuring its strength by how heroically it scrambles during a disaster and start measuring it by how effectively it prevents the crisis from reaching the hospital doors in the first place.
Ashiana Reaz works at Democracy International (DI) and writes on public policy, environmental, and public health issues.

item.title: A fight for our existence. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Last Friday, three of my colleagues visited Haji Mazar Basti in Tongi, on the outskirts of Dhaka, on a reporting assignment to expose an illicit drug trade that has operated there unabated for far too long. They had no idea that a sophisticated CCTV network run by the drug cartel was recording their entry into the slum alleys in real time. Inside, they found brisk, open trading in drugs of every kind in broad daylight, completely unchecked by the state’s law enforcement apparatus.
While investigating this open narcotics trade, the three-member team was ambushed by an armed gang of 20 to 25 people. The Dhaka Tribune journalists endured unimaginable torture at the hands of these drug ruffians, who held them captive for three hours, beat them, threatened their lives at gunpoint, and robbed them of their belongings.
Since that barbaric attack, very little has happened -- not that we expected much -- apart from our newspaper's truthful reporting on the trade, the filing of a police complaint, and strong assurances from senior police officials that raids would be conducted and legal action taken against the perpetrators.
Badly injured and mentally traumatized, the three victims are still undergoing medical treatment. One continues to suffer from lightheadedness and hearing impairment.
Local residents later told us that last Friday’s assault on the Dhaka Tribune team was one of the worst, though not the first, such incidents in Haji Mazar Basti. Recently, journalists from at least two other national dailies also fell victim to the same tyrants.
It is the very spot where retired serviceman KM Tahsif Sauri was last seen before his tragic death. Tahsif went missing after leaving his family’s residence in Uttara on the evening of October 27, 2026. The following afternoon, Tongi River Police recovered his body floating near Rajabari Ghat in the Turag River, identifying him through an iPhone and wristwatch found on his person.
I stand to be corrected, but to my knowledge, since the recovery of his body -- and the subsequent discovery of his motorbike near the slum -- there has been no official drive to dismantle this notorious drug den.
In writing this, I do not mean to suggest that our law enforcers never raid criminal hideouts. They do. And when they fail to act, we see episodes such as that involving former junior minister Ishraque Hossain, who recently took matters into his own hands to fight neighbourhood drug dealers -- an act that ultimately cost him his ministerial job.
No sane person would endorse a public official taking up arms to chase down drug dealers. Yet one can certainly empathize with his frustration after dozens of pleas at official coordination meetings went unheard and the police failed to meet basic public expectations.
The Ishraque episode is a telltale sign of how law enforcement agencies, and the higher-ups who direct them, have failed citizens who ask only that an elected government free their neighbourhoods from an ever-expanding drug network.
To be fair to our law enforcement agencies regarding Haji Mazar Basti, they have conducted special drives there in the recent past. In May this year, police arrested 38 people and uncovered a concealed, air-conditioned luxury drug den complete with an escape tunnel.
Two months later, police arrested 42 more suspects, seized heroin and yaba, and disconnected electricity and internet connections to roughly 300 rooms suspected of being used for drug trading. Then, in August, authorities conducted eviction drives, demolishing around 100 illegal structures used as drug dens.
This raises an obvious question: How does the gang keep returning to operate a sprawling narcotics business in the very same area, time and again?
To understand this, we must look at Bangladesh’s thriving political economy, where political patronage quickly comes to the aid of illicit operations whenever they face the wrath of law enforcement.
Allegations are rife that, regardless of who holds power in the central corridors of the state, narcotics dealers at strategic distribution points enjoy vital political protection from both sides of the political aisle. That protection gives them the audacity to intimidate, terrorize, and unleash violence against any journalist who dares to expose them.
Why, then, is the press so determined to expose the drug threat? The answer is simple: It is a fight for our very existence.
We are living dangerously in this country. If police records and media reports are any indication, scarcely a day goes by without news of drug addicts killing or injuring people -- most often family members who refuse to give them money for a fix or neighbours who try to stop them. If we collectively fail to halt the rapid spread of this thriving market, it will soon catch up with every one of us in one way or another.
I will refrain from naming the specific spots in Dhaka where drugs are readily available. All it takes to score is the urge for a kick, the cash to pay for it, and knowledge of the selling points.
The media today is awash with reports on these hotspots and their unchecked trade. Just the other day, I read about a Toyota Land Cruiser Prado carrying 300,000 yaba tablets that set out from Cox’s Bazar for Dhaka on August 17. After stopping in Chittagong for a day, the vehicle took the Dhaka-Chittagong highway before being intercepted by the district detective branch police in Comilla.
According to reports, nearly 2.7 million yaba tablets were seized in six major incidents along the Cox’s Bazar border in the preceding five months alone. Five of those consignments were destined for Dhaka, from where, according to investigation sources, the drugs were to be distributed nationwide. Law enforcement data show that the largest consignments entering through our borders are now routed through metropolitan areas before being distributed across the country.
At the same time, the country’s eight major cities -- Dhaka, Chittagong, Rajshahi, Gazipur, Rangpur, Khulna, Barisal, and Sylhet -- have emerged as massive drug markets in their own right, largely due to their dense populations.
Data from pending court cases reveal the scale of this urban spread. Official figures indicate that 47,948 serious drug cases, carrying minimum sentences of five years or more, are awaiting trial in these eight metropolitan areas, out of 166,333 such cases pending nationwide. Nearly 29% of Bangladesh’s most serious drug cases are concentrated in these eight cities.
Before drawing the urgent attention of those in high offices to this crisis, let us briefly review how Bangladesh reached a point where the drug menace has become so pervasive.
Recall 2018, when the then government embarked on a nationwide "war on drugs" -- around the same time that the controversial Digital Security Act was enforced despite fierce opposition from civil society, rights bodies, and journalists. Over the next two years, Bangladesh witnessed at least 500 to 1,000 deaths in controversial "crossfire" shootings.
Then, in 2020, the killing of a retired serviceman at the hands of rogue policemen -- allegedly on the payroll of narcotics traders -- sparked a nationwide outcry. It compelled the government to take a measure almost unheard of in contemporary world history: Withdrawing and replacing the entire police force of Cox’s Bazar district, comprising between 1,100 and 1,400 personnel.
Fast-forward to 2026. In August this year, our current home minister, who hails from Cox’s Bazar, acknowledged that yaba tablets entering across the border were being distributed nationwide, ruining a large section of our youth. He spoke of preparing an “impartial list” of top drug traffickers as part of the government’s effort to curb smuggling and strengthen narcotics control.
When we put all these developments together -- the widespread crossfire killings of the late 2010s, the withdrawal of an entire district’s police force, and the unabated narcotics trade stretching from Gendaria’s Ghuntighar (of Ishraque fame) to Tongi’s Haji Mazar Basti -- a clear pattern emerges.
It is a cycle of half-hearted administrative measures, repeated empty assurances, and a section of politicians profiting from the proceeds of a thriving illicit market. Slowly but surely, and perilously, this network is engulfing the country like a spiderweb.
Now, it is up to us to decide: Do we truly intend to free ourselves from the grip of this drug crisis, or will we allow it to destroy the future of our children and generations to come?
Reaz Ahmad is Editor, Dhaka Tribune.

item.description:
Tuba Hassan’s three-wicket haul and an unbeaten partnership between captain Muneeba Ali and Ayesha Zafar helped Pakistan beat Bangladesh by eight wickets in their Group ‘B’ match of the ICC Women’s Emerging Nations Trophy at the Karwan Sports Club Cricket Ground in Ajman on Thursday.

After opting to bowl, Pakistan restricted Bangladesh to 108-9 in their allotted 20 overs through a disciplined bowling performance led by Tuba, who claimed three wickets for 26 runs. Left-arm spinner Nashra Sundhu also impressed, taking two wickets for 13 runs.

Bangladesh appeared to be in a reasonable position at 52-2 before their innings suffered a dramatic collapse. They lost five wickets for just 16 runs as Pakistan tightened their grip on the match.

Tuba triggered the slide by dismissing Sharmin Akter for nine before removing Bangladesh captain Nigar Sultana Joty, who scored 27, and Ritu Moni for two.

Nashra provided further breakthroughs to keep the opposition under pressure, while Shorna Akter offered some resistance with an unbeaten 21 to help Bangladesh cross the 100-run mark. Nigar’s 27 remained the highest individual score for her side.

In reply, Pakistan made a brisk start, with Shawaal Zulfiqar striking four boundaries in a six-ball 16 before departing early.

Sadaf Shamas then steadied the innings with a valuable 37, helping Pakistan reach 68-2 at the halfway stage and keeping the required run rate comfortably within reach.

Captain Muneeba and Ayesha completed the chase without further loss, putting together an unbeaten 44-run stand for the third wicket.

Muneeba remained not out on 31, while Ayesha contributed an unbeaten 27 as Pakistan reached 112-2 in 15.5 overs, sealing victory with 25 balls to spare.

Bangladesh’s Sobhana Mostary and Shorna took one wicket apiece, but their efforts were insufficient to prevent Pakistan from securing a comprehensive win.

The victory was built on Pakistan’s effective bowling after Bangladesh had made a steady start, with Tuba’s strikes in the middle overs proving decisive.

Pakistan’s batters then ensured there was no late drama, completing the chase comfortably to strengthen their position in Group ‘B’.

item.title: PM Shehbaz highlights Pakistan's solar 'revolution by ordinary citizens' at COP31. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Wednesday highlighted Pakistan’s solar power boom at the COP31 in Turkiye, where world leaders gathered to discuss joint solutions to combat climate change.

This year’s summit focuses on transitioning toward a low-carbon future. Delegates from nearly 200 countries are meeting in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya as global greenhouse gas emissions show little sign of falling and wars, inflation and other crises compete for political attention.

Addressing a high-level dialogue on clean energy transition, titled ‘35 by 35: Powering the Future’, PM Shehbaz said: “In my country, an extraordinary transition has already taken place.

“In just two years, Pakistan has added nearly 22 gigawatts of rooftop solar capacity — a quiet revolution by ordinary citizens seeking affordable power and a cleaner, more predictable future.”

He affirmed that Pakistan fully supports the ‘35-by-35 Global Electrification Pledge’, wherein countries agree to aim to increase electricity’s share of total final energy consumption to around 35 per cent by 2035 in line with global climate objectives.

The premier recalled the recent inauguration of a “key section” of Pakistan’s seventh nuclear power plant, Chashma-5, referring to its dome placement. He explained that the project will add 1,200 megawatts of clean energy to Pakistan’s energy mix.

“A second transformation is now underway on our roads and highways. Clean sources now provide nearly 55pc of our energy mix,” PM Shehbaz declared.

The prime minister then highlighted that Pakistan’s newly drafted auto policy builds on the country’s aim to have 30pc of its new vehicles be electric by 2030 by offering “incentives for them through lower tariffs”.

“All future government buses and motorcycles will be electric. This year, for the first time, more than one in every 10 motorcycles sold in Pakistan was electric,” he stated.

“The momentum is real and it is accelerating,” PM Shehbaz remarked, while cautioning that “momentum without finance cannot be sustained”.

“Our grids must expand quickly and reliably. Storage must keep supply steady. New technologies must be affordable for all. Yet, this burden falls on countries already under heavy debt,” he emphasised.

The prime minister noted that Pakistan alone needs around $138 billion by 2035 for low-carbon power and $50 billion more to replace coal with solar.

He stated that the ‘35 by 35’ clean energy goal could only be achieved “if finance flows at the speed of ambition through concessional capital and the transfer of affordable technology”.

“Let us resolve to power our economies without impoverishing our people and light up our homes without darkening our planet. That is the promise of 35 by 35, and it is a promise we must deliver together and under all circumstances,” the premier remarked.

He thanked Turkiye President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, whose country has the COP31 presidency, for convening the “important dialogue”.

Earlier in the day, PM Shehbaz was received by Erdogan and UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres upon his arrival at the venue, the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) said.

The premier and other world leaders then gathered for a group photograph at the summit.

In his speech at the Antalya Leaders’ Summit, PM Shehbaz will highlight Pakistan’s climate priorities and emphasise the urgent need for enhanced global climate action and strengthened international cooperation to mitigate the adverse impacts of climate change, according to PMO.

The Foreign Office (FO) said the prime minister will also highlight “Pakistan’s steps towards rapid solarisation and expansion of its renewable energy capacity, as part of its transition towards a cleaner and more resilient economy, along with its efforts to strengthen disaster preparedness and early-warning systems”.

He will call for predictable, adequate and accessible climate finance for developing countries to strengthen their resilience and pursue sustainable development, it added.

According to the PMO, a “Pakistan Pavilion” has been established at the COP31 venue where 54 events will be hosted on various themes.

Turkiye’s Erdogan highlights Gaza ‘ecocide’

Dozens of leaders were to speak during the “high-level segment” taking place on Wednesday and Thursday, including Erdogan, Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian and Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, whose country hosted last year’s climate talks.

“Nature — no less than people — is also paying a heavy price for armed conflicts. The starkest example of this is Gaza… what has taken place in Gaza is not only a genocide, but it is also an ecocide,” Erdogan said to applause.

Turkiye did not invite Israel to COP31, The Jerusalem Post reported.

“As the host country for the leaders’ summit, we did not send an invitation to Israel,” it quoted Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum as saying.

“Of course, we will discuss the climate and climate justice here. We say that there can be no climate justice where peace does not prevail.”

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, Chinese Vice President Han Zheng, and the United Kingdom’s PM Andy Burnham were also scheduled to speak on Wednesday.

The United States, the world’s largest historical emitter, has skipped the talks for the second year in a ‌row after ⁠President Donald Trump — who has called global warming a hoax — withdrew the US from climate cooperation following his return to office in 2025.

Negotiators from nearly 200 countries are seeking agreement on a plan to increase the share of electricity in global energy use and revive stalled efforts to move away from fossil fuels.

As the third day began, the UN chief told world leaders at the summit that the slow international response to climate change so far had placed the world on a path to destruction.

Governments must fight harder to preserve the planet for future generations, he said, in comments that set the tone for two days of rapid-fire speeches by world leaders.

“The brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us. This is the path to mutually assured destruction,” Guterres said, pointing to rising emissions, global temperatures and worsening climate-driven disasters.

“But science is not telling us to surrender. It is telling us to fight harder.”

PM meets world leaders

On the sidelines of the summit, the prime minister held conversations with leaders of various countries and international bodies.

The premier and his delegation also had a separate meeting with Iran’s Pezeshkian and his team.

The meeting was to “discuss bilateral relations and the promotion of mutual cooperation between Pakistan and Iran”, as well as the regional situation and matters related to regional peace, PMO stated.

PM Shehbaz, in a post on X, said he was “delighted to meet my brother”.

While reaffirming the “deep and enduring bonds” between the two neighbours, the prime minister said he “conveyed Pakistan’s deep concern over the prolonged conflict in our region”.

“Dialogue, restraint, de-escalation and sustained diplomacy are the only path to lasting peace,” he stressed.

“Building on the understandings reached under the Islamabad MoU, Pakistan continues to play a sincere and constructive role for peace and stability in the region and beyond.”

PM Shehbaz also met with Kuwait’s PM Ahmad Al-Abdullah Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah, with both leaders discussing the longstanding fraternal relations between their countries.

They “reaffirmed their resolve to further strengthen cooperation in a range of areas of mutual interest, including trade, investment, energy, development cooperation and people-to-people exchanges”, PMO said.

The two premiers expressed the hope that the recent ratification of the Pak-Kuwait defence agreement would “further promote bilateral cooperation”. They also exchanged views on international developments and challenges to regional peace.

PM Shehbaz’s informal meetings included those with Bangladesh’s PM Tarique Rehman, Palestinian PM Mohammad Mustafa, Saudi Energy Minister Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud, Saudi State Minister for Foreign Affairs Adel bin Ahmed al-Jubeir and Syria’s President Ahmed al-Sharaa, according to PMO.

He also met Organisation of Islamic Cooperation chief Ismail Ould Cheikh Ahmed, World Bank President Ajay Banga and Türkiye’s First Lady Emine Erdoğan.

In his conversation with his Palestinian counterpart, PM Shehbaz expressed Pakistan’s full solidarity with Palestinians.

According to PMO, Mustafa thanked the government and people of Pakistan for “effectively raising their voices on the global level against the injustices inflicted on the Palestinian people and for supporting the Palestinian stance”.

“During these cordial meetings, the prime minister and the world leaders discussed strengthening bilateral relations and the situation in the region,” PMO said.

It added that the meetings also stressed the importance of highlighting the challenges faced by countries most affected by climate change at the international level.

Year of extreme weather

A UN report last month found the world on course to break through the 1.5 degrees Celsius warming limit that countries had agreed to pursue under the Paris Agreement to prevent the worst effects of climate change.

Meanwhile, 2026 has also stood out with a series of extreme heatwaves across Western Europe and a glacier collapse in Nepal that triggered a catastrophic flood killing more than 1,450 people, with thousands still missing.

Former French prime minister Laurent Fabius, who presided over the 2015 Paris climate conference and leads an advisory council of former COP presidents, said on Tuesday the leaders’ speeches should give political impetus to the negotiations.

“It is an opportunity for leaders to make some announcements, and more this time, to explain how they will implement, because the key word in Antalya is implementation,” he told Reuters.

Several other nations, including France, Germany, Japan, Italy and Canada, did not send their top leaders to the talks this year and won’t be represented in the speeches.

“The world’s biggest economies should be leading the response to the climate crisis, not leaving it to others,” said Mohamed Adow, director of climate and energy think tank Power Shift Africa.

Age of electricity?

COP31 host Turkiye has been pushing for countries to put a goal on electrification at the centre of a final deal, though critics say it may do little to curb warming.

The proposal targets a rise in electricity’s share of total global energy consumption to 35 per cent by 2035, up from a little over a fifth now, theoretically reducing greenhouse gas emissions from cars, factories and buildings.

But the proposal does not include language requiring new power to be generated by clean energy sources, and governments have yet to clarify a broader plan to transition away from fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas.

Guterres urged countries to speed their transition to clean energy sources.

He said the world’s dependence on fossil fuels was also damaging economies, not just the climate, an apparent nod to surging petroleum prices since the start of the US and Israeli war against Iran that has disrupted Middle East oil exports.

“Three-quarters of humanity live in countries that import fossil fuels, hostage to price shocks they did not create and cannot control,” he said.

“Recent conflicts make clear that this is a recipe for chronic insecurity and a cost-of-living meltdown.”

‘Difficult start’

Ahead of the conference, negotiators had been locked in discussions late on Sunday over demands by developing nations to include items on climate finance in the official agenda.

“This has already been a difficult start for COP31,” said Jasper Inventor, head of Greenpeace’s COP31 delegation.

Under UN climate agreements, developed countries, which are historically responsible for most greenhouse gas emissions, have provided financial support to help developing nations adapt to climate impacts and transition to cleaner energy. But poorer countries say the sums remain insufficient.

Inventor said developed countries were “taking a hard line” over whether to include a platform, agreed at COP30 in Brazil last year, aimed at discussing how wealthy nations should provide funds to developing nations.

African countries are also pushing for the agenda to include discussions on the tripling of adaptation finance, which aims to help poorer nations pay for measures such as building sea walls or planting drought-resistant crops.

Observers say few major breakthroughs are expected at COP31 as countries grapple with an oil price shock and geopolitical tensions fuelled by the US war on Iran and Russia’s conflict in Ukraine.

item.title: Concrete cannot replace the green. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The reopening of Osmani Udyan after nearly nine years of delays is certainly a positive for the capital.
With that said, that the cost escalated from Tk54-58 crore to an eye-watering Tk147 crore once again lays bare just how reckless we continue to be with public spending - funds that could have gone to countless other areas of need for this country.
With that said, a space such as this is a long-overdue development for Dhaka’s urban landscape. For a capital routinely ranked among the world’s least livable cities, the revival of a 23-acre open space is crucial.
Third spaces - parks, plazas, and public grounds - should never be seen as urban luxuries but rather as fundamental necessities for public health, mental well-being, and social cohesion, especially in a suffocating metropolis such as ours.
However, we do question the nature of this makeover and what was prioritized during planning. In stripping away mature shade trees and paving over natural soil to build expansive concrete walkways and structures, the Dhaka South City Corporation (DSCC) has compromised the park’s primary identity as a natural green refuge.
Replacing rich, cooling canopy trees with hard surfaces exacerbates the urban heat island effect rather than mitigating it. A park redevelopment project that reduces actual foliage in a city starved of greenery represents a fundamental misinterpretation of ecological design. Modernization should enhance natural ecosystems, not pave over them.
We need the authorities concerned to ensure that Osmani Udyan serves its true purpose. For that, the first order ought to be an urban afforestation drive within the park, planting native, shade-giving trees to restore its lost canopy. Furthermore, maintenance standards must be strictly enforced so that entry fees translate directly into a safe, pristine environment for all.
Dhaka desperately needs its third spaces, but they must remain genuinely green, maintained, and accessible to the people who need them most.

item.title: An attack on our values. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The directive issued by National Parliament Whip and Habiganj MP GK Gouse to potentially block Baul music and rural folk music events under the guise of preventing "obscenity" is a dangerous, deeply alarming overreach.
Demanding that law enforcement preemptively ban or restrict centuries-old folk traditions at the district level displays a staggering contempt for the secular, pluralistic fabric of this country’s identity.
When those entrusted with legislative authority want to deploy state machinery to police cultural expression, it sets a chilling precedent that emboldens intolerance and threatens to erase our rich heritage.
The Baul tradition of Bangladesh was included in the list of Masterpieces of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity by UNESCO. For generations, Baul, pala gaan, and folk traditions have preached peace, humanism, and syncretic harmony across our lands.
To conflate these indigenous art forms with morality violations or criminal misconduct is both intellectually dishonest and socially destructive.
If specific unlawful activities occur at any gathering, law enforcement agencies already possess the legal mandate to address individual infractions. Blanket bans, administrative intimidation, and arbitrarily denying event permits represent moral policing masquerading as governance.
State officials must remember that elected representatives are sworn to safeguard the constitutional rights of all citizens, not to enforce personal, regional, or moral dogmas upon the public.
Using district law and order committee meetings to weaponize administrative machinery against folk artists directly undermines cultural freedom and feeds into the very intolerance that fractures national unity.
These authoritarian directives that peddle populism have no place in a Bangladesh striving to be better. Local artists, folk musicians, and organizers must be protected and permitted to perform without fear of political harassment or interference.
The state’s duty is to defend our diverse heritage, not surrender public spaces to cultural erasure. Freedom of expression and the preservation of our traditions are non-negotiable pillars of what makes us Bangladesh. No public official should be permitted to dismantle them.

item.title: When lies go viral. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Today, people can hardly avoid social networking sites, smartphones, and the wider online environment. This growing vulnerability can distort public debate and weaken social trust. Human perception is psychological and develops through daily reactions to events, statements, and rumours. It is now shaped not just by oratory, print media, and television, but by a faster, more affective information landscape.
Often, fraudulent claims are presented as credible as Facebook posts, YouTube videos, TikTok snippets, fabricated news cards, and AI- generated material compete for attention. In Bangladesh, this risk has become clearer during political transition, election-related mobilization, student politics and debates over national sovereignty.
Information warfare and the cognitive battlefield
NATO's scientific advisory body describes cognitive warfare as manipulating an opponent's cognition to weaken the will and ability to make decisions. There are no boundaries in the conflict of information warfare. It entails manipulating, warping, magnifying, or suppressing information to affect public opinion. The parts of the human mind -- emotion, memory, fear, values and judgement -- are the primary targets.
The human mind therefore becomes the battlefield. The objective is not always to persuade individuals to believe a particular lie. A more effective objective may be to induce confusion. This undermines reasoned discussion and makes emotionally fulfilling narratives more appealing than substantiated facts.
In Bangladesh, information warfare typically operates in tandem, using multiple linked approaches:
Is Bangladesh at risk?
There is a large and active online population in Bangladesh, which is especially vulnerable to the issues of political polarization, social and religious sensitivities, and media literacy gap.
Information can be false and proliferate from platform to platform before being verified by authorities. Stories of religion, nationalism, violence, and social grievance can easily foster fear and anger, division and distrust.
Social media has great advantages to it. It provides rapid information, gives a voice to the voiceless, and uncovers the truth, where traditional media may fail. However, Facebook is also a hub for misinformation in Bangladesh due to this openness.
Rumour Scanner reported 4,195 instances of misinformation in 2025, which was approximately 30% percent higher than in 2024, out of which 3,806 were found on Facebook. It also recorded a highest monthly total of 521 cases in December 2025, 86% of which were political cases.
A malicious rumour can easily and rapidly break out from the screen and become a real threat. Accusations and reactions can be triggered well before the truth is known, by false allegations of religious insult, communities, child abductions, or even political conspiracies that can provoke crowds.
That is why it is not just what people believe which is dangerous, but what their beliefs can trigger.
It can be a community reaction -- fear of a neighbourhood, hostility between communities, pressure on public institutions, or lack of trust in public institutions.
The psychological damage may have occurred by the time that a rectification is supplied.
The layers of AI
Artificial intelligence has blurred the line between real and fabricated content online. AI-generated videos, manipulated images, and convincing fake messages can appear authentic, prompting people to believe and share them before checking the facts.
Before the February 2026 election, researchers found many AI-manipulated posts intended to mislead voters. Some invented events that never occurred; others used fake images or news cards designed to resemble genuine journalism.
Deepfake videos also showed political leaders making statements they had never made. Female candidates were targeted with sexually explicit fake images, while other AI content attempted to create fear between religious communities.
The real peril of AI is not that every machine-generated image will fool everyone, but that it has dramatically lowered the cost of producing convincing deception.
Once, creating a realistic fake video required specialized equipment, technical expertise, and substantial effort. Nowadays, there are tools that can create a fake voice, image or short video within minutes.
For ordinary users, and even for professional fact-checkers, the amount of suspicious content can be very difficult to identify. It also helps a malicious actor to dismiss true evidence as a deepfake, as the researchers call it, and therefore to benefit from a more general “liar's dividend.”
Cross-border relations exist as a challenge to it. In 2025, Rumour Scanner reported 155 cases of disinformation regarding Bangladesh that was spread by external media and social media accounts. The information battle is not restricted within the country’s boundaries, but the narratives from external sources affect the minds and psychology of Bangladeshis.
Misinformation, disinformation and malinformation
The terms are interchangeable, but the difference is important. Misinformation is inaccurate information or information that is false, but not necessarily done with purposeful intent. A person who sends a re-posted old flood video that purports to be from the current disaster, could be spreading misinformation.
Disinformation is information that is knowingly and intentionally false for the purpose of deceiving, influencing or harming someone. An example is a fabricated quote by a political leader.
Malinformation is factual information that has been taken out of its context to mislead, harm or sway, which includes revealing private information to intimidate.
A coordinated entity may create deception, and the general citizen may then disseminate misinformation, believing it to be truthful. An original picture can have a deceptive caption, turning a reality into a tool for deceit.
Recognizing these variations will enable the community to react intelligently. Not all incorrect information is from an enemy, it can be every unverified share that can reinforce a harmful campaign.
A theory of the origins of false beliefs
As psychology demonstrates, people tend to see, validate, and share what confirms their political, religious, or social opinions. They may not accept corrective information, as it threatens them with an attack on their identity or community.
Emotion intensifies the issue. Fear, indignation, and outrage reduces fact-checking. Therefore, rumours generally incite violence, religious feuds, threats to women, and children, or national sovereignty.
These are statements that are meant to develop feelings, not thinking. The message “share before it is deleted” or “the media will not show you this” creates an urgency and does not give time to think.
Repeatedly seeing a claim on Facebook, TikTok, YouTube, and message groups may lead to a false impression of truth. People are seeing what they already believe in, as like-minded pages and online groups form echo chambers. Fake news has a reach that is greater than fact-checks.
Lessons from the Bangladesh Army
Bangladesh Army regularly observes October of each year as Cyber Security Awareness Month. Various awareness programs, seminars, workshops, and training take place during this month, more than in any other month.
All offices and installations use the slogan on cyber protection on top of the letters issued or circulated. Instructions on security breaches through social media, awareness against misinformation, disinformation, and malinformation are circulated and communicated to everybody regularly in each darbar, central motivational parade, and so on.
Thus, individuals are now more aware, and they are encouraged to report a security breach whenever it has been noticed.
The shared responsibility and the way forward
Independent fact-checking organizations like Rumor Scanner and FactWatch provide a valuable public record of false claims. Before a correction is issued, a deepfake video may reach a very large audience.
Thus, an effective response is necessary, and it must be timely and transparent. The news outlets should have verification desks and make clear corrections to readers and indicate how they were reached. We also need technology platforms to make synthetic content transparent and take effective action against concerted efforts of manipulation.
However, citizens too have a critical role to play in controlling misinformation. There must be questions asked before sharing a sensational post like: Who published it first? Do credible sources support the claim? Is the post evidence or an incitement to anger and urgency? A reverse image search, a fact check of the original source, or a fact check on a trusted fact-checking website can often prevent false information from spreading. Cognitive warfare in Bangladesh will continue, but public resistance can render manipulation much less effective. AI could be utilized to identify suspicious content at the earliest. Platforms, journalists, fact-checkers, and authorities can take a coordinated approach to verify them based on common guidelines. Media literacy and responsible journalism are also essential to public trust and these are tools that can help to enhance the response.
Colonel ASM Nazmul Haque, psc is in the Bangladesh Army.

item.title: Why are the malls empty?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The most revealing feature of Dhaka’s struggling shopping malls is not the number of closed shutters, but the hesitation behind them. A market may have merchandise on its shelves, staff waiting behind counters and discounts displayed, yet customers can walk past.
The decline in activity at established destinations such as Eastern Plaza, Eastern Mallika, Mouchak Market, Police Plaza, and Shah Ali Plaza, alongside the closure of Karnaphuli Garden City, invites a larger question: What happens when consumers lose not only the capacity to spend, but also the confidence to do so?
It is easy to explain the retreat by pointing to online shopping and the arrival of newer commercial complexes. Both have altered the retail landscape. Digital platforms allow customers to compare prices, browse products and arrange delivery without negotiating Dhaka’s traffic.
Modern malls offer facilities that older markets may lack. Yet these changes explain where people shop, not necessarily why they are buying less.
When traders across different locations report falling sales, vacant shops, and difficulty meeting rent and salaries, the issue cannot be reduced to a competition between physical and digital stores. It points to a weakening of demand across the marketplace.
The pressure begins in the household budget. Food, housing, transport, education, healthcare, and utility bills claim first place because they cannot easily be postponed.
Clothing, cosmetics, shoes, jewellery and household upgrades come later. When the cost of essentials rises faster than income, discretionary purchases become the first casualties.
Families may continue to buy what they need, but they buy less frequently, choose cheaper alternatives, repair rather than replace, or simply wait. The absence of a customer in a shop may therefore represent a decision made long before that person reaches the market: The household has already decided that the purchase can no longer be justified.
This is the difference between having money and having disposable income. A person may receive the same salary as before and still feel poorer because that salary commands fewer goods and services.
Retailers face the reverse side of the same squeeze. Imported products become more expensive, while rent, electricity, wages, and service charges add to operating costs.
A shopkeeper cannot indefinitely absorb these increases. Prices rise, but customers whose incomes have not kept pace resist them. Traders are caught between costs they cannot control and buyers who cannot afford the prices required to cover those costs. Offering a discount may attract attention, but it cannot solve a structural loss of purchasing power.
The psychology of this retreat deserves as much attention as its arithmetic. Consumers do not make every decision by comparing prices and calculating immediate utility. They also respond to fear, expectations, habits, and the possibility of future hardship.
A family uncertain about employment, medical expenses, or next month’s bills may avoid spending even when it has some money left. Savings become a buffer against risks that feel increasingly difficult to predict. The pleasure of buying something new competes with the reassurance of keeping cash available. In uncertain times, reassurance often wins.
Behavioural economics offers a useful explanation. Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky’s prospect theory argues that people assess outcomes relative to a reference point and that losses can carry greater psychological weight than equivalent gains.
Their memorable formulation, “losses loom larger than gains,” helps explain why a consumer may experience spending as a potential loss of security rather than simply an exchange of money for a product.
The prospect of enjoying a new pair of shoes may seem modest beside the fear of being unable to meet an unexpected expense. The decision not to buy is then not evidence of indifference to consumption; it is a response to perceived vulnerability.
Another relevant concept is loss aversion, which can make consumers particularly sensitive to price increases. A product that once cost Tk 1,000 but now costs Tk 1,400 is not experienced merely as a new market price. The increase can feel like a loss of purchasing power, especially when wages remain unchanged.
Even if the item is still affordable in absolute terms, the buyer may resent paying more and postpone the purchase. Repeated price shocks can gradually reset expectations. Consumers begin to regard older spending habits as excessive and develop a more restrictive idea of what is necessary.
Richard Thaler’s work on behavioural economics also challenges the assumption that people behave like perfectly rational economic actors. His distinction between “econs” and “humans” captures the gap between theoretical decision-makers and actual people, whose choices are shaped by context and emotion.
A shopper may respond to a discount, but may also avoid a purchase because the household budget feels fragile. A retailer who assumes that lower prices alone will restore demand may misunderstand the customer’s real calculation.
The consumer is not simply asking whether an item is cheaper today; the consumer is asking whether buying it will create anxiety tomorrow.
There are, of course, problems within the retail sector itself. Some older shopping complexes have failed to maintain facilities or adapt to changing expectations. Poor ventilation, inactive escalators, neglected common areas, limited product variety, and weak customer service can make a visit less attractive. Buyers increasingly expect convenient payment options, reliable products, transparent prices, and the ability to compare alternatives.
A mall that once enjoyed prestige cannot depend indefinitely on its history. The difficulties of older complexes therefore reflect both an economic squeeze and a failure by some businesses and property managers to renew the shopping experience.
The damage does not stop at the shop counter. Retail connects importers, manufacturers, wholesalers, transport operators, delivery workers, landlords, and employees. When sales decline, retailers reduce orders.
Suppliers carry less stock, manufacturers may cut production, and businesses under pressure may reduce staff or delay investment. Lost jobs and lower incomes then weaken demand further.
A decline in consumption can thus become a cycle: Households spend less, businesses earn less, employment becomes less secure, and households become even more cautious. Empty corridors are only the visible part of a much wider chain.
This is why the condition of shopping malls should not be dismissed as nostalgia for an older style of shopping.
Karnaphuli Garden City’s closure is a reminder that commercial property cannot survive on its location or reputation alone. Nor should every struggling market be treated as proof that consumers have moved online.
The more important question is whether people across income groups have enough confidence and financial room to participate in ordinary consumption. A transfer of purchases from a physical shop to a website is a change in channel. A household abandoning purchases altogether is a sign of economic contraction.
Policy must therefore address the conditions that shape consumer confidence. Controlling inflation, creating secure employment, protecting real wages, ensuring fair competition, and reducing the burden of essential services are not merely social objectives; they are foundations of a functioning domestic market.
Reliable information and predictable economic management also matter because uncertainty influences spending decisions. Retailers, for their part, must improve facilities, use digital channels intelligently, maintain transparent pricing, and respond to customers with different budgets.
Neither public policy nor commercial innovation can guarantee success for every shop, but both can help create an environment in which demand has room to recover.
The quietness of Dhaka’s shopping malls is ultimately a story about the relationship between income, expectation, and trust in the future. People do not stop wanting attractive clothes, comfortable homes, or small pleasures simply because a market has changed.
They stop buying when the cost of those pleasures appears too high against the risks they face. Behind a vacant shop is a household making choices about food, rent, tuition, medicine, and the next uncertain month.
When ordinary purchases begin to feel financially dangerous, the crisis belongs not only to retailers. It belongs to an economy whose consumers are losing the freedom to spend.
HM Nazmul Alam is an academic, journalist, and political analyst based in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Currently he is teaching at IUBAT.

item.title: Pakistan beat Nepal to set up U-19 Asia Cup semi-final against Bangladesh. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Defending champions Pakistan maintained their unbeaten run in the ACC Men’s U-19 Asia Cup 2026 with a convincing 101-run victory over Nepal at the Al Amerat Cricket Ground in Muscat on Tuesday.

With three wins from as many matches, Pakistan finished top of Group A to qualify for the semi-finals, where they will take on Bangladesh in the first semi-final on Thursday.

Batting first, Pakistan posted 275-7 in their allotted 50 overs, with half-centuries from Ahmed Hussain and captain Farhan Yousaf laying the foundation for the total.

Ahmed top-scored with a brisk 89 off 73 balls, hitting seven fours and two sixes, while Farhan contributed 74 off 95 balls, including six fours and three sixes.

The pair steadied the innings after Pakistan had slipped to 64-3, adding 135 runs for the fourth wicket. Hasnain Abbas Dar provided late impetus with a quick-fire 25 off 23 balls.

For Nepal, Bipin Sharma took three wickets for 58 runs.

In reply, Nepal were bowled out for 174 in 43.4 overs. Ahmed completed an impressive all-round performance, claiming four wickets for 35 runs in his 10 overs. Mohammad Huzaifa and Mohammad Sayyam took two wickets each.

Rohit Chand was Nepal’s top scorer with 37.
