item.title: Ensuring safety on roads is necessary. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Nearly 300 families wiped out in road accidents over six years and ten months is a devastating reflection of the state of road safety in Bangladesh -- figures that represent hundreds of lives lost, children left without parents, parents who have lost their children, and families whose lives have been permanently changed.
According to a recent analysis by the Road Safety Foundation, accidents involving motorcycles, auto-rickshaws, microbuses, private cars, and other vehicles have increasingly resulted in multiple members of the same family being killed together. The findings point to a number of persistent problems, including reckless driving, unfit vehicles, inadequate driver training, and widespread disregard for traffic laws.
These are not new concerns. Yet, despite repeated reports, road accidents continue to claim lives at an alarming rate.
We cannot keep treating these deaths as inevitable consequences of travelling on our roads. Most of the contributing factors are preventable, and that makes the continued loss of life even more unacceptable.
The authorities must take a more comprehensive approach to road safety. Vehicle fitness certification must be strictly enforced, particularly for microbuses and ambulances. Drivers must receive proper training, and those who operate vehicles for excessively long hours without adequate rest must be held accountable. The movement of battery-run rickshaws on highways also requires urgent attention.
At the same time, safer road designs, proper dividers, service roads, and better monitoring are essential. Traffic laws must be enforced consistently, regardless of who is behind the wheel. Public awareness campaigns should also emphasize responsible driving and the importance of quality helmets for both motorcyclists and passengers.
Ultimately, road safety must become a national priority rather than a recurring discussion after every major accident.
Every journey should not carry the possibility of an entire family being lost. The government must act with urgency, strengthen accountability, and ensure that our roads become safer for everyone.

item.title: Who is behind Dhaka's terror?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The growing wave of violence across Dhaka, with attacks near police stations, government buildings and university campuses, has created an atmosphere of fear and uncertainty that cannot be allowed to continue. More than 50 crude bomb explosions and at least eight buses set on fire in recent days should be enough to sound the alarm.
What is particularly concerning is how little we know about those responsible. While police have reported arrests and ongoing investigations, the larger questions remain unanswered: Who is organizing these attacks, where the explosives are coming from, who is financing the perpetrators, and what they are hoping to achieve.
These are questions that demand urgent and credible answers, and the government and law enforcement agencies must get to the bottom of this fast. Investigations cannot become an endless cycle of statements about operations and arrests without tangible results. Authorities must identify not only those carrying out the attacks but also the people financing, supplying, and directing them. CCTV footage, intelligence gathering, and coordinated police operations must be used effectively to establish the full network behind this violence.
At the same time, arrests must be based on evidence, not political affiliations or suspicion. Holding the right people accountable is essential, but indiscriminate action will only undermine public confidence in law enforcement.
More importantly, the government must do everything within its power to remove the growing sense of fear and insecurity gripping the country. People should not have to worry about their safety when travelling to work, attending university, or simply going about their daily lives.
Stronger security measures, visible police presence, and timely public communication are imperative to restoring confidence. Violence and intimidation cannot become an accepted part of everyday life.
The public deserves to know who is behind these attacks and what is being done to stop them, and the government must act decisively before this situation deteriorates further.
Restoring public safety must be an immediate priority.

item.title: Dhaka: Miles to go before we sleep. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Where do you get the best city views from the metro rail? For me, it is certainly the green and watery western side of Uttara. Then comes the stretch from Agargaon to Bijoy Sarani, with the open space of the old airport and the relatively low-density areas around Sher-e-Bangla Agricultural University and the National Parliament House. And, of course, the brief but beautiful view of Dhaka University.
What makes these views special? Not just the buildings, but the breathing space between them.
In a well-planned city, you do not simply build buildings. You preserve open land, trees, wetlands, parks and public spaces where people can walk, breathe, meet, play and do absolutely nothing. A city should not demand that every inch of land generate economic returns. But beyond a few remaining green spaces and institutional areas, where is the land available to ordinary citizens for greenery, water bodies, public parks or simply an open stretch of ground?
We are struggling to build more concrete walls, install more air conditioners, consume more energy and emit more carbon. We are replacing natural cooling systems with mechanical ones, then paying the price through electricity bills, heat and pollution. This might sound rude or selfish, but we are literally digging our own grave.
Dhaka has a rich history stretching back centuries, and its muslin was once renowned around the world. Yet look at the city we are building today.
Dhaka ranked 171st out of 173 cities in the Economist Intelligence Unit's 2025 Global Liveability Index, making it the third least liveable city in that assessment. Meanwhile, the World Bank's 2024 environmental analysis reported that air pollution, unsafe water, poor sanitation and hygiene, and lead exposure collectively cause more than 272,000 premature deaths annually in Bangladesh. These are not just statistics; they are a reminder of the price we pay for neglecting our living environment.
The disappearance of canals and wetlands, the endless excavation of roads during the monsoon, the burden of traffic, poor waste management and the deterioration of air quality are leaving a lasting impact on everyone who lives here and takes the next breath.
Living a peaceful life should not be a luxury. Yet in Dhaka, it often feels like a privilege reserved for those who can afford to escape its worst conditions.
After midnight, you might hear loudspeakers from a neighbourhood event. The city never truly sleeps, and its residents rarely stop running. They work to pay rent, school and tuition fees, medical bills, food expenses and transport costs. Even rest becomes something people struggle to afford.
Where are the parks for our children? Where can our elderly people walk safely, during the day or at night? Across much of the city, pavements are inadequate, obstructed or occupied by shops, vendors and parked vehicles. Certain planned neighbourhoods enjoy better walking environments, but access to clean air, safe pavements and green spaces should not depend on one's postcode or income.
The ordinary resident deserves the same dignity.
Dhaka's metro rail offers a glimpse of what is possible when infrastructure connects people. But a city is not just about transport, buildings and roads. It is also about the quality of life between destinations: the trees we walk under, the water bodies we preserve, the parks where children play and the open spaces where communities come together.
And this brings me to a bigger question: Why must so much of Bangladesh's administration, investment, employment, and decision-making remain concentrated in Dhaka?
The government should seriously consider relocating the Secretariat to a suitable site farther out, within a properly planned growth corridor or an expanded Detailed Area Plan (DAP) area. Rather than shifting administrative functions from one congested part of Dhaka to another, we should use this opportunity to rethink how the capital grows.
But relocation must not become another excuse to destroy wetlands, clear green land or build a new administrative island surrounded by congestion. It should be supported by public transport, housing, environmental safeguards and essential services.
More importantly, moving the Secretariat alone will not decentralize Bangladesh. Government agencies, businesses, universities, healthcare facilities and employment opportunities must gradually become more geographically distributed. Other cities need the investment and infrastructure to become attractive places to live and work. People should not have to move to Dhaka simply to access a decent job, quality education or specialised healthcare.
We do not need to choose between development and nature. We need development that understands the value of public space, protects our natural environment and recognizes the limits of a city that keeps absorbing people, capital and opportunities without creating enough room for life.
Dhaka has a history worth protecting and a future worth fighting for. Those green and open stretches visible from the metro should not remain beautiful exceptions in an increasingly concrete city. They should remind us of what we still have and what we must protect.
Bangladesh is too centralized around Dhaka. It is time to expand opportunities beyond the capital, and preserve the remaining breathing.
Arif Hossain is the Executive Director of Farming Future Bangladesh and Regional Head of Asia at WePlanet International. He is a former Visiting Fellow at Cornell University and a Global Fellow at Michigan State University. Email: arif.hossain@weplanet.org

item.title: Bangladesh deserves better than a cycle of crisis. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
There is something deeply unsettling about watching a country with extraordinary potential repeatedly struggle to move beyond the same cycle of confrontation, uncertainty, and disruption.
Bangladesh is a nation built on resilience, sacrifice, and determination. Yet, somewhere along our journey, we seem to have developed an unfortunate tendency to allow disagreements to escalate into crises, crises into national spectacles, and national spectacles into narratives that overshadow everything we have worked so hard to achieve.
And often, the greatest casualty is Bangladesh itself.
Recent disruptions across our industrial areas have once again reminded us how vulnerable our economic progress remains to instability. Behind every factory are thousands of livelihoods, years of investment, international commitments, and the aspirations of people who have worked tirelessly to establish Bangladesh as a major global apparel exporter.
When production stops, the consequences travel far beyond factory gates. They affect supply chains, international commitments, investor confidence, and ultimately the country's reputation.
In today's competitive global economy, perception matters almost as much as performance.
Disagreements are inevitable in any society undergoing political, economic, and social transformation. The challenge is not their existence, but how we respond to them.
Too often, legitimate concerns become entangled with speculation, misinformation, political narratives, and unnecessary exaggeration. Isolated incidents can be presented as national emergencies, while meaningful conversations are lost beneath sensationalism.
This does not mean grievances should be ignored. Workers deserve justice, citizens deserve accountability, and institutions must remain open to criticism.
But there is an important distinction between raising concerns responsibly and amplifying them without considering the consequences.
International partners do not always distinguish between isolated incidents and systemic instability. What reaches them are headlines, images of unrest, and recurring signals of uncertainty.
We must ask ourselves whether we are allowing these narratives to define Bangladesh more prominently than its achievements.
Working closely with Bangladesh's ready-made garment industry has given me the opportunity to witness its achievements alongside its challenges.
I have seen manufacturers investing in sustainability, responsible business practices, environmental performance, and innovation. I have also witnessed the immense pressure businesses face from rising costs, changing international requirements, and global competition.
There is certainly much that needs improvement.
Workers deserve dignity, fair treatment, safe workplaces, and effective grievance mechanisms. Businesses deserve stability, predictable policies, and fair commercial opportunities. International buyers must also acknowledge their responsibilities in supporting the transitions they demand.
These interests are not contradictory. They are interconnected.
An industry cannot prosper sustainably by neglecting its workers. Equally, employment security becomes increasingly difficult when enterprises cannot operate consistently.
Our responsibility is to build an environment where economic competitiveness and social justice reinforce one another.
While we remain occupied with recurring domestic disruptions, the global economy is transforming rapidly.
Artificial intelligence, automation, climate change, supply-chain transparency, and sustainability requirements are redefining competitiveness.
Other countries are investing in technology, education, innovation, and higher-value industries.
Bangladesh must be equally ambitious.
Our national conversations should increasingly focus on productivity, workforce development, export diversification, responsible investment, and institutional strengthening.
We should be debating how to create better jobs, improve industrial efficiency, develop future-ready skills, and strengthen Bangladesh's position in global value chains.
Instead, too much of our collective energy continues to be consumed by managing crises that could often be addressed through timely dialogue and responsible leadership.
The opportunity cost of this distraction is enormous.
I often wonder whether we have begun confusing patriotism with the intensity of our opinions rather than the responsibility of our actions.
Loving one's country does not mean defending every institutional failure. Nor does demanding change justify undermining the achievements of millions.
True patriotism requires acknowledging shortcomings without diminishing progress, demanding accountability without encouraging destruction, and understanding that national development is a shared responsibility.
Our moral and spiritual values teach us justice, restraint, honesty, and accountability. These principles should guide not only our personal lives but also our public discourse.
Justice does not require hostility. Disagreement does not require humiliation. And progress cannot be built upon perpetual distrust.
As a development practitioner, I want Bangladesh to be recognized for innovation, responsible industries, economic resilience, and intellectual capability.
As a citizen, I want institutions that inspire confidence and a society where disagreements are resolved through dialogue.
And as a mother, I want the next generation to inherit a country where opportunities are created rather than repeatedly interrupted by instability.
Bangladesh has already demonstrated what collective determination can accomplish.
Imagine what we could achieve if that same determination were directed toward education, innovation, productivity, and sustainable development.
We have spent decades proving that we can survive adversity.
Perhaps it is time to prove that we can also prevent unnecessary adversity and build prosperity together.
Bangladesh does not need a future without disagreement. It needs a future where disagreement does not repeatedly come at the expense of development.
And that responsibility belongs to all of us.
Sheikh Shuchita Jahan Sneha is a development and industry specialist.

item.title: Bangladesh's external debt increases almost threefold in decade. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Bangladesh’s foreign debt has almost tripled in 10 years, a steeper rise than in any other South Asian country except the Maldives, according to the World Bank.

Even so, the country has a lower debt burden relative to export earnings than Pakistan, Sri Lanka and Bhutan. However, its burden is higher than that of India and Nepal.

According to the World Bank’s International Debt Report 2026, Bangladesh’s total foreign debt stood at $113 billion at the end of 2025, up from about $38 billion in 2015. That is the third-largest stock in South Asia.For every $100 in annual earnings, Bangladesh carries $210 in total debt and pays back $16 annually.

Economists say the indicators are manageable for now, but Bangladesh could face repayment trouble if borrowing keeps growing at this pace and the money is not put to proper use.

In the South Asia region, India holds the largest external debt stock at $764 billion, up 59pc in a decade. Pakistan follows at $135 billion, almost double the level of 10 years ago.

In Sri Lanka, foreign loans rose 31pc to $57 billion. External debt rose 186.5pc to $11 billion in Nepal and 57pc to $3.3 billion in Bhutan. The Maldives recorded a more than fourfold increase to $4.7 billion.

Repayments take 16pc of exports

Debt servicing took 16pc of Bangladesh’s export earnings in 2025, 3.1 percentage points less than the year before. That is the share of export income spent on repaying principal and interest on foreign loans, and a falling ratio is a positive sign of repayment capacity.

Even so, it remains above India and the South Asian average of 10pc, though below Sri Lanka at 26pc and Bhutan at 19pc. Measured against gross national income (GNI), servicing costs are low. At 2pc, Bangladesh matches India and the regional benchmark, against 5pc in Sri Lanka and 6pc in Bhutan.

The country’s debt-to-GNI ratio, which is external debt as a percentage of the national income, stands at 24pc. It is a manageable level but slightly above the South Asian aggregate of 21pc. The ratio is 20pc in India, 41pc in Pakistan and 54pc in Sri Lanka. Set against what the country earns from exports, the debt looks heavier.

External debt stands at 210pc of Bangladesh’s annual exports, more than twice what the country earns each year from foreign trade and other income.

That is far above India at 83pc and the South Asian aggregate of 95pc, but below Pakistan at 324pc, Bhutan at 301pc and Sri Lanka at 272pc.

Warning on borrowing

Zahid Hussain, a former lead economist at the World Bank’s Dhaka office, said Bangladesh still does better than Pakistan and Sri Lanka on these indicators but trails India. “If foreign debt keeps growing at the current pace, it would not be surprising if Bangladesh eventually faced a situation similar to Sri Lanka’s,” said the economist.

“If you are not prudent about the types of debt you take and how you use the borrowed funds, becoming another Sri Lanka is only a matter of time.” He said comparing Bangladesh with Pakistan is difficult, given Pakistan’s particular geopolitical and strategic situation.

Zahid said exports matter because the debt-to-GDP ratio shows very little about a country’s ability to repay. A large economy is not enough; it also needs adequate liquidity, which is why the export ratio is important.

On this measure, Bangladesh is also vulnerable because its export base is small and heavily dependent on a single product category. Its exports as a share of GDP are among the lowest, he said.

“Remittances add to foreign currency earnings, but even counting them India stays far ahead because its remittance income is much higher. Sri Lanka, similarly, receives large numbers of tourists and earns substantial foreign currency from tourism,” he added.

Costlier loans ahead

Prof Mustafizur Rahman, a distinguished fellow at local think tank Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD), said the debt-to-GDP and debt-to-export ratios are rising gradually, but the most important indicator is the ratio of net exports to debt servicing.

He said that about 85pc of export earnings come from readymade garments, where domestic value addition is 60-65pc. The ratios would therefore be significantly higher if net exports were used.

Recent loans carry relatively high interest rates and shorter repayment and grace periods, so the ratios will rise rapidly in the coming years, said Mustafizur, as Bangladesh already faces growing debt pressure. Government debt servicing was $4.9 billion in the last fiscal year and is projected to reach $7.6 billion by 2029, as interest rates climb while grace and repayment periods shrink. The interest rate in Japan, for example, has risen from below 1pc in 2021 to above 3pc, he said.

He said Bangladesh needs to raise exports and domestic value addition, improve domestic resource mobilisation and reduce its reliance on foreign borrowing to finance the Annual Development Programme.

“Global financing conditions are tightening. Bangladesh will still need foreign loans, but should negotiate better terms and secure more concessional financing,” he said, adding, “It could also consider raising funds through bond issuance.”

According to the World Bank report, foreign debt of developing countries rose 5.5pc to a record $9.4 trillion in 2025, the fastest growth since 2021 and about four times the average pace of 2022-24.

Debt-service pressure remained severe amid elevated global interest rates. Low and middle-income countries paid $1.4 trillion in principal and interest in 2025, up 1.9pc and the fifth consecutive annual rise.

Between 2022 and 2025, developing countries paid $436 billion more in debt service than they received in new financing.—The Daily Star/

item.title: 21 killed as migrant boat sinks off Senegal. [ dawn ]
item.description:
DAKAR: A small boat carrying migrants sank off northwestern Senegal killing at least 21 people in the latest tragedy along the dangerous Atlantic Ocean route from Africa to Europe, authorities said.

The Senegalese interior ministry said that only one person had been rescued in addition to the 21 bodies recovered, which added to the thousands who have died in recent years trying to reach Spain’s Canary Islands from West Africa.

The ministry said the death toll was “provisional” and that the search was still going on. Media reports said the pirogue-type flat-bottom boat capsized on Saturday off the Loumpoul dunes in Kebemer department, between Dak­ar and the northern city of Saint-Louis.

However Saliou Diouf, founder of Senegal’s main migrant aid association Boza Fii, said that “the sinking occurred on Friday”. The nationalities of all the victims had not been confirmed, he said.

Greek coastguards rescue 28 from migrant boat off Crete

“But the bodies recovered yesterday (Saturday) are Senegalese,” he added. Thousands of people from We­­st Africa try each year to reach Eur­­ope on the perilous Atlantic route.

Senegalese authorities also said they had intercepted 142 migrants on Friday who were on a similar small boat aiming to reach Spain.

The group included 23 women, two babies and two other children, and were from Senegal, Gambia, Guinea-Bissau, Guinea and Nigeria, according to police. The Senegalese government on Saturday stressed “its determination to combat people smuggling networks, notably through strengthened cooperation with neighbouring countries,” the interior ministry said in a statement.

Spanish authorities on the Canary Island of El Hierro declared an emergency on Saturday after a surge in migrant boat arrivals.

Boat in distress

Greek coastguards said on Sunday rescuers had found the body of a man and dragged to safety 28 other people on a migrant boat in distress off the island of Crete.

Maritime police launched an eme­rgency rescue after the boat issued an alarm signal, with winds of 40-50 kilometres an hour making sea conditions difficult, the coastguard said.

The survivors, all reportedly Sudanese, were picked up by another boat sailing nearby, then transferred to a police vessel and taken to the port of Heraklion on Crete, the agency said. On Wednesday, 59 people were reported missing after their boat capsized off the island, according to a 23-year-old Bangladeshi man who survived. No bodies have yet been found.

item.title: Journalists across Asia face police action in growing crackdown on movements. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
“I was put in a bus. I showed them that I have an ID card and a mic ID, and asked them why I was being detained. But they didn’t want us to show how protesters were being manhandled,” said 28-year-old Pragya Mishra, who runs a news outlet called Ulta Chasma uc.
On October 11, 2026, Mishra was covering the protests against Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar at RK Ashram in Delhi. While reporting, Mishra says her cameraperson Anuj Kumar (23) was pulled by his hair by police personnel. When she went to protect him and inform the police that they were from the media, she was also forcibly put inside a bus with a few other journalists.
She told Asian Dispatch that she was being taken to a detention centre in Rajendra Nagar. The bus, however, was intercepted and stopped by other journalists. She says that the police eventually dropped them at Connaught Place.
Mishra was not the only journalist who faced police action during the recent protests held across the country against Kumar over the alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the electoral rolls.
The protest against CEC Kumar is linked to the alleged irregularities in the ongoing SIR process, which has reportedly resulted in the deletion of around 13 crore names from electoral rolls.
It gained momentum after a report published by The Indian Express dated September 24 found that Election Commissioners Sukhir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had formally objected at least 14 times over a 10-month period.
According to the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), at least 43 instances of journalists being detained were recorded. Journalists from several news organizations such as The Wire, Scroll, The Quint, Newslaundry, as well as freelance journalists were detained -- some were even heckled, assaulted, and forced to delete what they had documented on the ground.
The Press Club of India, along with other journalists’ associations, condemned the detentions and said that the police took the step even after journalists displayed their press cards.
It further mentioned that the police seized the phones and reporting equipment of some of the journalists. The statement referred to the developments as a “blatant attack on the freedom of the press.”
Commenting on the situation, Reporters Without Borders (RSF) told us: “What we are witnessing is not simply excessive policing during demonstrations, it is part of a broader pattern of restrictions that undermines the ability of journalists to report freely on matters of public interest, particularly when their reporting exposes the conduct of the authorities.”
RSF is an international non-profit working towards protecting the rights of journalists/press. According to their 2026 World Press Freedom Index , India ranks 157 out of 180 countries in press freedom. The body also highlighted that press freedom remains a major concern across Asia, where the media faces restrictions in covering politically sensitive events and protests.
CPJ’s annual report on jailed journalists, released in January 2026, noted that 330 journalists were behind the bars globally as of December 1, 2025. Of these, one-third were in Asia -- China and Myanmar were found to be the leading jailers in the region.
It’s important to note that this number from Asia excludes jailed journalists from Central and West Asia (referred to as the Middle East in the graph). Those are marked separately in CPJ’s database.
Speaking to Asian Dispatch , Kunal Majumder, Asia-Pacific program coordinator, Committee to Project Journalists (CPJ), said that journalism is under attack across the region and added: “In South Asia, the focus is largely on over-regulation of the online space; apart from SLAPP [Strategic Lawsuits Against Public Participation] suits, physical violence remains a grave problem.”
Expressing concern about the situation in India, Majumder said that India has a responsibility to uphold press freedom and “serve as a role model for other countries in the Global South.”
This pattern where journalists have faced action, have been assaulted, detained or arrested by law enforcement agencies is consistent across other Asian countries.
For instance: the situation for journalists in Bangladesh during the 2024 July uprising was alarming. The International Federation of Journalists (IFJ) estimated that at least 160 journalists were reportedly injured while covering the nationwide protests as of July 31, 2024.
RSF noted that five journalists were allegedly killed by police bullets between July 15, 2024 and August 5, 2024, and one was killed during clashes between two factions.
CPJ, in a report published on July 26, 2024, detailed the reports of police attacks on journalists. It said that on July 16, 2024, police personnel fired metal pellets at journalists Mehedi Mamun, Abdur Rahman Khan Sarjil, Wajahatul Islam, and Jubayer Ahmed. This happened despite them identifying themselves as journalists.
The next day, July 17, 2024, Abdullah Al Mamum, a correspondent with Prothom Alo, was reportedly beaten with rifles and batons by police personnel while he was recording the police action against students. Mamum told CPJ that he showed them his press card but he was beaten and the police fired a rubber bullet at him while he was trying to flee.
More recently, Ernest Cruz, a reporter working with Bulatlat in the Philippines, was assaulted by the Quezon City Police on October 19, 2026, while he was covering a protest led by farmer groups. According to RSF, Cruz was assaulted despite identifying himself as a journalist.
A similar incident happened on September 21, 2025, when eight journalists covering the anti-government protests in Manila were harassed, assaulted, and obstructed. They alleged that police used shields to deliberately obstruct media coverage. The usage of tear gas and water cannons near to where journalists were also posed direct harm to their safety.
At least nine journalists in Sri Lanka were injured during the anti-government protests in 2022. A freelance journalist, Sumedha Sanjeewa Gallage, was reportedly attacked by the police while he was covering a demonstration outside the president’s residence. As per reports , he lost partial vision in his right eye following the attack.
The 2026 CPJ analysis also found that the greatest incidence of torture and beatings of journalists has occurred in Iran since 1992. Between 2022 and 2025, 71 journalists were imprisoned in Iran.
Mishra, who was bundled in a bus in New Delhi on October 11, highlighted that these detentions happened despite the Supreme Court clearly stating that lawyers and journalists should be allowed to work without hindrance.
“The Supreme Court had ordered that journalists, lawyers, and doctors should be allowed to continue their work…I pointed this out, but they [police] weren’t listening,” Mishra says. She also told us that she repeatedly asked the police personnel not to carry her and that she could walk to the bus, but nobody heard her.
Speaking about the detentions and the force with which journalists were met, RSF said, “The circumstances strongly suggest that journalists were targeted precisely because they were documenting what was happening on the ground: the police's brutal treatment of protesters. Several journalists were detained while filming arrests or acts of police violence. Others had their phones seized, their cameras damaged or were pressured to delete their footage. This raises serious concerns that the objective was to prevent images of police operations from reaching the public.”
Several journalists, who were covering the protests, also highlighted on social media that the police was asking for government accredited press cards and not recognising cards issued by independent organizations.
“ This raises fundamental concerns, press freedom cannot be conditional on government approval, and accreditation requirements must never become a tool for excluding independent or critical voices. The right to report does not depend on whether a journalist works for an established newspaper, an independent online outlet or a digital platform. All journalists must receive equal protection, regardless of their employer and professional status,” RSF said.
In Bangladesh, IFJ documented an expansion of gatekeeping intended to restrict the media’s ability to report. The Press Information Department had revoked the accreditation of around 167 journalists between October 29, 2024 and November 7, 2024.
These measures often lead to self-censorship .
The United Nations’ Human Rights Committee, in 2020 , adopted general comment number 37 that noted that the right to peaceful assembly should be recognized. It also highlighted the obligations of state parties regarding the same.
It said that law enforcement officials must respect and ensure the exercise of fundamental rights of organisers and participants, while also protecting journalists, observers, and others from harm.
The committee further said, “The role of journalists, human rights defenders, election monitors and others involved in monitoring or reporting on assemblies is of particular importance for the full enjoyment of the right of peaceful assembly.” It added that journalists and participants have the right to record law enforcement officials.
Majumder emphasised that every journalist has an equal right to report on public events without intimidation, obstruction, or discrimination. “The police must not decide who gets to do their job based on which media organisation they represent or what their reporting might reveal. Press freedom means protecting the right of all journalists to report, including those whose coverage may be critical of the authorities,” he said.
With respect to what happened in India, RSF recommended that courts should provide effective and timely remedies when journalists’ rights are violated, and newsrooms should strengthen safety protocols. It also said that the police must put an end to physical assaults, intimidation and the confiscation of journalistic equipment.
“Let us do our jobs. We don’t want any special or VIP treatment. We already go through a lot when we are on the ground…If the fourth pillar of democracy, which is journalism, is weakened, then what will happen to democracy?” said Mishra.
Abhishek is the associate editor at Asian Dispatch. Previously, he worked as the senior correspondent, fact-check for The Quint. The story was originally published by Asian Dispatch on October 22, 2026, and has been republished by Dhaka Tribune with permission.

item.title: Borrowing for our future. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The World Bank’s support to improve the quality of primary education and address learning gaps among children in Bangladesh is certainly positive news.
Aimed at improving learning outcomes, upgrading classrooms, providing essential learning materials, and strengthening school management for over 26 million children from pre-primary to Grade 5, we must be thankful that steps are being taken to improve the quality of a system where World Bank data show that around 50% of 10-year-old children in the country cannot read and understand a simple text appropriate for their age and grade level.
With that said, the approval of the $300 million financing package, while undeniably being a critical injection of resources into our foundational schooling system, must be recognized for what it is.
Every time international loans are secured for public development, a familiar shadow looms over the country: The deep-seated fear of administrative waste, corruption, bureaucratic leakage, and poor execution.
For decades, foreign-funded projects, regardless of the sector they are in, have too often been characterized by inflated costs and delayed rollouts that fail to bring about meaningful transformation.
Pouring hundreds of millions of dollars without ironclad execution safeguards is an unacceptable gamble. As such, the authorities concerned must recognize that this funding carries a heavy moral and economic obligation.
Every single taka must be channeled directly into measurable pedagogical improvements. There is no room for procurement corruption or administrative foot-dragging.
Foreign loans must build the nation’s future, not line the pockets of the influential and powerful, or disappear into bureaucratic black holes. If we are going to borrow to educate our children, we must ensure the investment delivers a measurable return -- transforming public primary education from a broken system into one that adds to our prosperity.

item.title: Holding the world accountable for the climate crisis. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
As world leaders assemble in Antalya, Türkiye, for the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31), it is safe to say that the threat of climate change has long ceased to be an abstract projection and has become the most significant existential catastrophe for the entire planet.
This is particularly true for a nation such as ours. With global heat records continuously shattered and fragile coastal ecosystems buckling under systemic salinization and relentless riverine erosion, Bangladesh remains among the most affected nations - due to a crisis it had virtually no part in creating.
For decades, global climate summits have yielded ambitious rhetoric, bureaucratic inertia, and pledges devoid of enforcement. At COP31, our diplomatic delegation, and indeed others from the Global South, must enter negotiations not to petition for international goodwill, but to demand the immediate, enforceable execution of climate justice.
The bedrock of our negotiating must reflect the economic reality we face as a result of climate change. Bangladeshi leadership must resolutely hold the world’s primary industrial polluters, ie the Global North accountable.
At a time when Bangladesh is experiencing among its most challenging economic issues, the effects of climate change continue to destroy infrastructure, deplete agricultural yields, and cause mass human displacement. Yet, it has been sad to see international countermeasures remain egregiously disproportionate.
The global Loss and Damage Fund, which was secured after years of arduous diplomacy, remains severely undercapitalized, with current allocation frameworks failing to address the true scope of vulnerability.
At COP31, Bangladesh must lead the coalition of climate-vulnerable states in advocating for legally binding financial commitments and doing away with the unreliable paradigm of voluntary contributions that major economies routinely disregard.
Beyond loss and damage, we must also prioritize direct, grant-based adaptation capital. Bangladesh cannot continue to accept climate finance structured as debt-bearing loans, which serve only to exacerbate existing foreign reserve strains.
Global climate equity is not optional, and COP31 must mark a turning point where Bangladesh plays its part in compelling the international community to honour its obligations.

item.title: The muddying of the waters. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humayun Kabir, when answering journalists’ questions on various serious subjects, often tries to create a little humor with some sarcasm and mockery.
Recently, Kabir was asked whether former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina had applied for a passport to return to the country. The question can’t be called entirely reasonable, since there has been nothing to suggest that Hasina has applied for a passport at all.
In other words, the person about whom the passport question is being asked has herself said nothing about a passport. Anyway, if a journalist is curious, they will naturally ask, and a responsible official could be expected to give a proper answer.
The state minister said he knows nothing about a passport. Of course, he wouldn’t, because Sheikh Hasina has said nothing about a passport or a travel pass. Kabir, however, did not stop there.
“Is she going to come here to visit her in-laws’ home in Rangpur, that I should give her a passport, and she’ll come with the passport?” He described the matter as “laughable.” Then he laid out the government’s position in his own words.
“Sheikh Hasina is a fugitive terrorist. A dictator, a runaway terrorist,” he said.
Kabir’s choice of words here is quite interesting. Humayun Kabir is a Britain-based expatriate, so he knows well what “terrorist” means in the Western world. There, “terrorist” mainly means Islamist militants (although in the United States some armed white supremacist groups are designated as “domestic terrorist” organizations). Here a suspicion remains that, by labeling Hasina a “terrorist,” the minister wants to create an image of her in the minds of Westerners.
On bringing Hasina back from India, Kabir stood firm on his earlier position. “We have an active extradition treaty for catching terrorists, for catching criminals,” he said. “To catch terrorists and criminals, you don’t need a passport; they are handed over.”
He is right about this. The very purpose of the extradition treaty between Bangladesh and India is to arrest each other’s “terrorists” and “criminals” and send them back.
The problem lies elsewhere. Does India see Sheikh Hasina as a “terrorist” or “criminal” at all?
From the answer that Indian High Commissioner Dinesh Trivedi recently gave to a university student’s question at an event, no one should have any doubt that the Indian government, far from considering Sheikh Hasina a terrorist or criminal, treats her with considerable respect. Throughout his entire statement, Trivedi addressed the former PM as “Hasinaji.” Those with even the slightest idea of Indian social customs know that in that country, no responsible person adds “ ji ” to the name of a criminal or terrorist.
Is a passport a citizen’s right?
Trivedi had said that Hasina came to India on August 5, 2024 as the prime minister of Bangladesh. He also said the Indian Air Force did not “rescue” her from Ganabhaban. It was Bangladesh’s own military that took her to Delhi for her safety.
If India does not see Hasina as a “terrorist” or “criminal,” there is considerable room for doubt about whether the extradition treaty, however active, would apply in her case.
There is a second problem with Humayun Kabir’s statement. The government’s spokesperson and the Prime Minister’s Adviser on Policy and Strategy, Zahed Ur Rahman, said something slightly different a day earlier.
When he was asked multiple questions on the same subject at his regular press briefing, he did not directly rule out the possibility of giving Hasina a passport. He said he knows Hasina has made no such application, and that the government has no plan sitting ready.
“If it were the case that she (Hasina) had asked for it (a passport), then what the government would do, I think it is better to keep that to answer at that time.”
Rahman’s reply lightly touches on another aspect, whose importance is immense. He brought up the issue of citizenship, and he spoke of “this state,” that is, the state that was founded under the leadership of Hasina’s father.
Leaving the country and coming back is the constitutional right of all citizens of “this state” -- getting the document needed for travel, that is, a passport, is also their right. But under Bangladeshi law, in certain cases a citizen’s passport can be canceled, and they can be barred from leaving the country, and likewise an application for a passport can be rejected.
But canceling or rejecting a passport is all done to stop someone from leaving the country. The matter of returning to the country from abroad remains somewhat murky.
Extradition versus return
Hundreds of cases have been filed against Sheikh Hasina; one or two have been “tried” in her absence, and she has even been given the death sentence. The government considers Hasina a “fugitive,” so surely the government would want her to return and come under the country’s law?
Since Hasina has expressed a wish to return voluntarily in December, that apparently seems the easiest and quickest path. On the other hand, the extradition that Humayun Kabir speaks of, which Zahed Ur Rahman dramatically explains as “we will bring her by catching her,” is a long legal process; nobody can say how many months, or even years, the extradition process might take.
And even after the process ends, there is no guarantee that the Indian government will actually hand Sheikh Hasina over to face the death sentence.
Against this background, if the government chooses the long extradition process as the only road, and dismisses the possibility of a quick return with some absurd remark, then only one conclusion can be drawn: The government in fact does not want Sheikh Hasina to return to the country. That is, the government does not want the verdict in Hasina’s concluded trial to be carried out.
Listening to the state minister, it does not seem that Hasina’s presence in the country is desirable to the government. There could be two reasons.
First, in the current situation, the government has neither the political courage nor the strength to carry out the verdict against Sheikh Hasina.
Second, Hasina’s return would, on the one hand, revive the Awami League, and on the other, push the anger of Jamaat-e-Islami and the NCP to its peak. Perhaps the BNP lacks the confidence to face this two-sided political challenge.
Sabir Mustafa is the former head of BBC Bangla and is currently working as a freelance journalist and podcaster. Views expressed are the author’s own.

item.title: The future of biodiversity relies on shared consensus. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Governments, civil society, scientists, youth, academia, artists, and media professionals gathered under the theme of 'Taking Action for Nature' at COP17 Armenia to bring about collective action on biodiversity protection and nature restoration.
Reviewing targets and protocols
COP17 Armenia conducted the first global review of the collective implementation progress of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KMGBF). The KMGBF is set on 23 global biodiversity targets which are to be completed by 2030 in line with the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety and the Nagoya Protocol on Access and Benefit Sharing (ABS).
Targets two and three, restoring 30% of all degraded ecosystems and conserving and effectively managing 30% of land, waters, and seas, respectively, took precedence in the KMGBF discussions. There has also been significant discourse on how KMGBF can be financed, how actors and stakeholders responsible for it can be accountable, and how its credibility can be ensured.
Strengthening biosafety by monitoring living modified organisms (LMO), reduction of invasive alien species, compliance and accountability, monitoring and evaluation, and ensuring gender equality and gender-responsive approach for biodiversity action were also discussed.
There was little difference in technical opinion on biodiversity protection, but there is hesitation in resource mobilization and funding implementation.
These conversations generated three critical questions:
The commitment to address these grand questions is there, but the scale, strength, and pace of the decisions are not enough.
One reason is the slow implementation of the National Biodiversity Strategies and Action Plans (NBSAP) adopted by countries around the world. Another reason is the current economic and geopolitical trend. Their connection to biodiversity damage is not talked about enough.
The current global biodiversity funding gap stands at $700 billion. The GEF-9 Replenishment was announced, where new countries pledged close to $4.4bn. This barely scratches the surface of the gap. The CALI Fund adopted in COP16 Cali, Colombia garnered a lot of attention. It was initially created to collect private-sector contributions from industries that rely on genetic data in nature, for example big pharma, biotech companies, cosmetics giants, etc.
However, voluntary contributions have been measly. No major corporation contributed to the CALI Fund. Participants mainly talked about ensuring fair and equitable commercialisation and benefit-sharing of genetic data.
The polarity of financing perspectives is a recurring challenge that raises questions. Developing countries seek international finance to do the work. Developed countries, on the other hand, urged diversification of funding sources.
But how can we generate financial mechanisms that ensure direct access to local communities? How can we combine grants, loans, and other financial instruments to develop these mechanisms? How can we achieve more transparency in these processes?
The rights of nature and people
Target 18 of the KMGBF, which is reducing incentives and subsidies harmful for biodiversity by at least $500bn (for example phasing out pesticides) and introducing positive incentives without affecting biodiversity was up for debate and requires great political will.
This also applies to biodiversity-protected areas. There are calls to ensure improved and practical ecosystem development, biodiversity protection coordinated with livelihoods, community rights, and equitable governance.
One way is to acknowledge the legal rights of nature. Advocates explained how ecosystems and species have legal rights just like humans. This puts nature as a living entity at equal legal footing with humans, not as their property, such as Panama's Rights of Nature Law adopted in 2023.
Corporations harming these rights would be violating law. Such perspectives and laws can better support conservation and biodiversity protection, but inclusive implementation with women, youth, and indigenous communities is important here.
Aligning actions around the Rio Conventions
Integrating climate action and biodiversity action without duplicating mandates is fundamental if we are to address all three Rio Conventions -- climate change, desertification, and biodiversity.There was no structured discourse on Rio synergy in the conference.
There were talks about carbon trading and how local communities can participate and benefit from carbon trading marketplaces. If their ownership, stake, and decision-making remain, they can manage natural resources best without overexploitation. It will allow countries to maintain the carbon credit trade and reduce emissions sustainably.
For Bangladesh to make use of this market, mangrove restoration and wetland conservation are great areas to start.
The use of technology and AI in developing biodiversity information systems was met with optimism. Armenia and Colombia jointly committed to finance endangered species conservation through private sector engagement. There is hope to achieve all 23 targets by 2030, but things still do not look too good.
From a Global South perspective, we raised concerns about how biodiversity conservation should complement livelihoods, respect community experiences, and engage people of faith.
We must consider the Rio synergies, and we must ensure multi-stakeholder governance and multilateral cooperation. We urged governments and experts to create a structured method to measure impact on ecosystem recovery, species conservation status, livelihood resilience outcomes, and equitable benefit sharing.
Science should be able to influence policy-making and economics and create tripartite solutions. We have committed to nature, to the world, and to the people with the KMGBF. Without its implementation, we are failing ourselves.
Will the global review lead to stronger, measurable action before 2030? Will biodiversity finance and governance genuinely empower local communities?
The world does not need another declaration of concern about biodiversity loss. While we saw great progress in technical aspects, the success of that progress truly depends on political consensus.
If governments together can adopt these technical perspectives and put them into proper funding pathways, policy, and practice, there is hope for the future of biodiversity.
Kazi Amdadul Hoque is the Senior Director, Strategic Planning & Head of Climate Action at Friendship.

item.title: SAFF Championship: Pakistan cruise past Maldives 3-0, close in on semi-final spot. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Pakistan revived their semi-final hopes in the SAFF Championship with a commanding 3-0 victory over Maldives in their second Group B fixture at the National Football Stadium in Dhaka on Sunday.

A first-half brace from Najeebullah Bettani, alongside an early penalty converted by McKeal Aroon Abdullah, helped Pakistan register their first victory of the tournament and put themselves in a strong position to qualify for the last four.

Pakistan made an aggressive start and took the lead in the fourth minute when they were awarded a penalty.

McKeal Abdullah stepped up and calmly converted from the spot to give the Green Shirts an early advantage.

Pakistan continued to press forward and doubled their lead through Najeebullah, who produced a well-timed finish after Junaid Shah delivered an excellent cross from the left.

Najeebullah made a perfectly timed run into the box, got ahead of his marker and poked the ball home.

The forward then completed his brace with a superb individual effort. With Pakistan defending deep in their own half, the ball was cleared upfield, where Najeebullah brought it under control on the right before unleashing a powerful strike past the helpless Maldives goalkeeper.

Pakistan’s three-goal advantage at half-time reflected their attacking efficiency, with the side making the most of their opportunities to put the contest beyond their opponents.

Despite enjoying slightly more possession, Maldives struggled to translate it into meaningful attacking opportunities.

Pakistan, meanwhile, were more threatening in front of goal, registering 15 shots, including five on target, compared to Maldives’ seven attempts, only one of which tested the goalkeeper.

Both sides pushed for more goals after the interval, but neither could find the breakthrough as the second half ended goalless, leaving Pakistan with a convincing 3-0 victory.

The result marked a significant response from Pakistan following their 3-2 defeat against arch-rivals India in their opening Group B encounter on November 5.

Pakistan had trailed 3-0 at half-time in that match before producing a spirited late comeback.

Najeebullah and Alamgir Ghazi scored in stoppage time to reduce the deficit, but India held on to secure all three points.

The 2026 SAFF Championship, running from Nov 5 to 17 in Bangladesh, features six participating teams divided into two groups. Group ‘B’ comprises Pakistan, India and Maldives, while hosts Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Bhutan are in Group ‘A’.

The top two teams from each group will advance to the semi-finals.

With their victory over Maldives, Pakistan have moved into a stronger position in the qualification race but must now wait for the outcome of the remaining Group ‘B’ fixture between India and Maldives, scheduled for Nov 11.

Maldives will need a substantial victory over India to overtake Pakistan in the group standings and secure qualification.

Otherwise, Pakistan and India will progress to the semi-finals.

For Pakistan, the emphatic win provides a timely boost after their opening defeat and puts them within touching distance of a place in the last four.

item.title: Expanding the public transport network. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The government’s announcement to construct two monorail corridors across the capital by 2030 -- with BUET consultants completing pre-feasibility studies and detailed designs underway -- is certainly a welcome step in expanding Dhaka's public transportation network.
Designed to complement the existing Metro Rail and address last-mile connectivity in high-density bottlenecks, this appears a sensible undertaking to offer a viable, eco-friendly solution to chronic traffic gridlock that only seems to worsen in the capital.
Expanding mass transit has long been an absolute necessity for economic survival in the city, and it is good to see plans being developed to address it.
Yet, public enthusiasm for new transit infrastructure is inevitably tempered by a history of systemic mismanagement, and this apprehension is not without reason.
For decades, Bangladesh’s megaprojects have been plagued by a predictable blueprint of failure: Severe deadline extensions, rampant cost overruns, poor coordination, and opaque procurement processes that balloon into crushing public debts.
When major infrastructure ventures consistently double their original budgets, often as a result of incompetence, disregard, or simple administrative inertia, it is taxpayers who carry that unfair financial burden.
The proposed monorail initiative, and indeed subsequent infrastructure projects, must break decisively from this legacy of inefficiency. If this project suffers the same bureaucratic bloat and inflated expenditures that have tarnished past endeavours, its primary rationale will be completely compromised.
We must thus establish uncompromising governance from day one. The government must set firm, non-negotiable cost caps and strict timeline milestones, holding contractors and public officials accountable for any unjustified delays or financial leakages.
Building modern transit for Dhaka is a crucial step forward and has no alternative. However, it is doing it on time, within budget, and free of corruption that must be ensured.

item.title: Feeding children is just good economics. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Economics divides itself into two. Macroeconomics is about how the whole economy works, and it's what we always see the talking heads on TV chattering away about. Inflation, the deficit, interest rates, and so on. Macroeconomics is also the part of economics we don't know much about, and much of what we think we do is wrong.
Microeconomics is the details of prices and markets and interactions between people. Much of what we know here is correct even if many people would prefer that it weren't. For many people would much prefer it if humans didn't go around acting so human all the time.
Those words, macro and micro, also give us a clue. Macro means large, micro small. So, if you want to be a big and important person -- or a talking head on TV -- then you'll want to lean on macroeconomics. You know, chatter on about the big stuff.
But the bit that really makes the difference to how life is lived is that small stuff. As is true in life itself of course -- it's the little things that make life enjoyable and worth living. Further, with micro, we can do experiments and really zero in on what actually works.
The news is that the Bangladeshi government has understood one part of this sort of research and is even doing the right thing about it. It's this : “The government's school feeding initiative is set for a major expansion in 2027, with plans to increase coverage from 3.1 million to around 11 million students at government primary schools across the country.”
We could just say that parents should feed their kids at home and that's that. We could also say that isn't it great that the kids get a lovely meal from the government? But that's not really the point or issue here, it's this: “Ensuring student attendance.”
A lot of research has been done on who sends their kids to school and why. One alarming result was that when child labour is made illegal, then fewer poor children go to school. The logic is that some people are so really poor that any child has to start work so that that child brings in enough money to feed that very same child.
Poor parents know that education is a good thing, it will make the children richer when they're older. But it is necessary for that child to survive long enough to get older.
Research shows that such poor families might well send one or some of the children to school and others have to go to work in order to bring in the necessary money to feed all of them. Of course, it will be more likely to be girls who are made to work while the boys learn to read and write.
If we make child labour illegal, then this will lower the wages the children can receive when working. This is obvious and logical as people will exploit those working illegally more than those working legally. If the wages of the children working fall, more of the children have to work to be able to feed all of the children.
Note that economics is not saying this should happen. It's certainly not approving of it happening. It's just noting that this does happen.
We'd prefer there to be no child labour, of course we would. But as we see, just making it illegal can actually increase the amount of it.
So perhaps we require a different way of achieving our goal?
One of the basic findings of that whole field of microeconomics is that people respond to incentives. In fact, Charlie Munger (he was Warren Buffett's partner) used to say: “Show me the incentive and I'll tell you the outcome.”
Another way of putting that same point is that we should try to tempt people to do the right thing rather than attempt to force them. You know, promising a toddler a sweetie often works better than slapping them in getting them to do something.
So, to restate the poor children and school problem. The parents can only feed the child if the child works, so therefore the child doesn't go to school and is thus trapped in lifelong poverty.
What if we feed the child at school? Then they will both be fed and also be educated? And this time, all the kids can go to school because all the kids will be fed.
This has been studied a lot. There are whole shelves of research in libraries on this. As far as anyone can tell, this works really well.
The World Food Program from the Americans pays for this in many countries and is going to help in Bangladesh. There's also a charity, Mary's Meals, which does the same thing for whole countries. The charity does it possibly better and certainly cheaper than the government, but that's another story.
We've got something that is going to make that future world better. Children will be fed, that's good, but also more children will gain more education.
I personally don't like macroeconomics but a lot of that is because I simply cannot get my head around the advanced mathematics used in it. A failing of mine rather than the subject perhaps.
But I also like this microeconomics because it provides answers to how to make the world a better place in simple, pragmatic, doable ways.
We can just feed every child at school. Feeding every child at school works, makes the world a better place in the future. So, we should do that then.

item.title: What makes growth inclusive?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
In recent times, there are renewed talks on the notion of inclusive growth. One question that keeps on popping up is what makes growth inclusive.
Everyone agrees that sustained economic growth is central to the ability of countries to advance human development and tackle poverty over a long period of time. But sustained growth alone is not enough to advance human development. For that, growth needs to be inclusive.
Inclusive growth is characterized by three mutually reinforcing elements:
Sustained growth which is pro-poor ensures poverty reduction as well as reduction in inequalities. Equity in resources, services, and income not only leads to human capabilities and opportunities, but it is also crucial for fair and just societies.
When growth is accompanied by rapid increases in productive employment, the incomes of and opportunities for the poor are likely to increase. Productive employment enhances livelihood, participation, dignity, and voice.
All together, inclusive growth is a driving force for human development and the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
To start with sustained growth is a prerequisite for inclusive growth. But sustained growth does not automatically become inclusive. In order to be inclusive, growth has to be pro-poor.
What is pro-poor growth?
The simplest notion of pro-poor growth assumes that so long as growth is associated with a reduction in poverty, it is pro-poor. The problem with this simple definition is that economic growth has largely been found to have some poverty-reducing impacts, at least through its trickledown effects. Thus, in terms of this simple definition, almost all economic growth is pro-poor.
The fundamental point, however, is that the “pro-poorness” of growth is not defined only by its poverty reduction impacts, but by the fact whether the poor actively engage in generating the growth, and also derive disproportionate benefits from it.
In other words, for growth to be pro-poor, the rate of income growth of the poor must exceed the rate of income growth of the non-poor and growth must accompanied by decreasing inequality.
While pro-poor growth is a necessary condition for inclusive growth, it is not a sufficient condition because it may not include non-poor people belonging to ethnic minorities, specific races, and so on. In many cases, these groups of people undertake economic activities which result in good livelihoods, but they have neither a voice in the decision-making process in the mainstream growth, nor are their activities integrated in it.
Equity remains at the heart of inclusive growth as distribution determines the pace, nature, and the pattern of growth. For growth to be inclusive, equity needs to be ensured on three planes:
If the production and the growth process start with an equitable distribution of assets, resources, and endowments, not only would they result in higher growth, but the benefits of growth are also equitably distributed.
When poor farmers have access to land and agricultural input packages, or small-scale entrepreneurs have access to credit, these not only enhance the growth process, but also ensure their fair share in it.
Infrastructure like roads, energy, transport, and communication has an economic activation effect, which implies new economic opportunities, better access to markets, and information. When poor people have access to such infrastructure, it makes growth pro-poor and inclusive.
Equitable access to basic social services, such as health and education and infrastructure, is another central factor for inclusive growth. The theoretical underpinning of this argument can be traced back to Amartya Sen’s work: Development as Freedom .
Inclusiveness effectively means eliminating the various “unfreedoms” experienced by individuals. According to Sen, people’s freedoms are enhanced through the provision of essential social services. Enhancing these freedoms is itself a precondition for achieving inclusive growth. An inclusive growth strategy, therefore, ensures that growth is promoted along with policies that enhance access to social services such as health and education.
In the realm of equity, redistribution of income is also associated with inclusive growth. This works on two fronts.
First , a redistribution of growth benefits the poor through enhancing their income, building their asset base, and enhancing their opportunities -- all of which ensure more inclusion of them in the growth process.
Second , a redistribution of income in various forms of social assistance to marginalized groups (eg, people with disabilities, older people), who cannot participate in the growth process, would provide social protection to them. These people are not part of the generation of growth but still become included in it as beneficiaries.
With regard to equity, two other observations may be pertinent in the context of inclusive growth.
First , equity is also a determining factor of the extent to which economic growth may impact poverty reduction. Initial inequality and changes in inequality are also important factors which can limit the extent to which poor people can participate in and benefit from growth.
Second , gender inequality impacts inclusive growth as well. Gender inequality in education and employment not only has a negative impact on economic growth, but it also adversely affects the pro-poorness of such growth. Also, significant gender gaps in access to agricultural productive assets and input such as land, fertilizer, and modern technologies seriously limit pro-poor growth.
Productive employment is a major driving force for inclusive growth. If growth is to be inclusive, it must be job-creating. This is because productive employment ensures people’s participation in the growth process, both as active agents as well as significant beneficiaries. And poor people can effectively be employed if economic growth is generated in sectors where they are concentrated and if labour-intensive technologies are used.
These linkages remind us of the importance of the sectoral composition of growth. The expansion of capital-intensive mining industries can result in jobless growth, making little impression on poverty. The incomes of the poor largely depend on the nature and extent of employment that economic growth generates.
It basically implies that not all growth is equally employment-intensive and there is no automatic link between economic growth and employment generation. Economic growth can be jobless, as the history of economic development has often shown.
Dr Selim Jahan is Former Director, Human Development Report Office and Poverty Division, United Nations Development Program, New York, USA.

The growing threat of unclean air. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Dhaka's air pollution has once again reached alarming levels, with the capital recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) of 203 on Friday morning. Classified as “very unhealthy,” this reading is another reminder of a public health crisis that continues to receive far less attention than it deserves.
Air pollution is not a seasonal inconvenience that residents should simply learn to live with. It is a serious threat to public health, contributing to respiratory illnesses, cardiovascular diseases, and other long-term complications. Children, older people, and those with existing health conditions are particularly vulnerable, but the consequences extend to everyone who breathes the city's air.
The sources of this pollution are well known: Unregulated construction, road dust, emissions from ageing vehicles, industrial pollution, and brick kilns all contribute to the problem. Yet, despite repeated warnings and directives, meaningful improvements remain difficult to see.
The courts have previously issued directives to tackle air pollution, including controlling construction dust and shutting down illegal brick kilns. The continued deterioration of air quality raises serious questions about how effectively these measures are being enforced.
We need more than occasional drives and temporary interventions. Authorities must coordinate their efforts, enforce environmental regulations and hold those responsible for pollution accountable.
Construction sites must follow dust-control requirements, illegal brick kilns must be shut down, and vehicle emissions must be monitored more strictly. Regular monitoring and transparent reporting should also become standard practice.
At the same time, improving public transport, expanding green spaces, and investing in sustainable urban planning must be treated as long-term priorities.
People should not have to choose between going outside and protecting their health.
Let us be clear: Clean air is a basic necessity, not a privilege. Dhaka's worsening pollution demands urgent, sustained action. Another day of alarming AQI readings should not remain another day of inaction.

item.title: We need more public-private partnership. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
A healthcare system under unrealistic pressure like ours needs practical ways to improve the quality and reach of public hospitals, and this initiative, if implemented carefully, could address some of the gaps that have long undermined public healthcare.
Under the proposed pilot, private partners will provide services at five tertiary-level hospitals, with fees still to be finalized before the program begins.
The intention to expand the model to other cities is also encouraging. Public hospitals face shortages of equipment, specialized services, and trained personnel. Private expertise and investment could improve facilities, strengthen management, and give patients access to treatment that might otherwise be out of reach.
However, this partnership must strengthen public healthcare, not make essential treatment a privilege. Fees charged by private partners need to be reasonable and clearly disclosed. Patients should not face unexpected costs, and those unable to afford additional charges must not be pushed aside.
The government must set firm standards for service quality, monitor performance, and hold partners accountable for meeting agreed targets.
The initiative must also complement sustained public investment. Bangladesh cannot rely on private participation alone to resolve long standing weaknesses in healthcare.
Hospitals need adequate staffing, functioning equipment, regular maintenance and better management. Plans to recruit more doctors and expand critical care facilities must move forward without unnecessary delays.
The five-hospital pilot should be an opportunity to measure results and correct shortcomings before expansion. The government must publish clear information on costs, services and outcomes so the public can judge whether the program is working.
This is precisely the kind of practical initiative the health sector needs more of. With transparency, affordability, and proper oversight, partnerships can help deliver better care to more people.
The real test, however, will be whether patients experience meaningful improvements.
